what kind of file it is
no, only the start
yes: says gzip compressed data


wc -l f
counting lines
yes
no; gunzip -c f \| wc -l












CautionMisconception: “To see what is in a file, I open it in an editor”



Reality. Large files can freeze an editor, and compressed ones show noise. head, less, and file let you look without loading the whole file; zless and gunzip -c … | head read compressed text.



Check yourself. A colleague’s 4 GB counts.tsv freezes their editor. How do you see the column names and the first rows?






TipAnswer





head -n 5 counts.tsv, which reads only the start. Or browse with less -S counts.tsv, which does not load the whole file at the start and keeps wide rows on one line.

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.11 History and shortcuts
Bash remembers what you type. Press UpUp a few times: earlier commands come back, ready to run with EnterEnter or to edit first. To see a numbered list of recent ones:


Terminal (laptop)

history | tail

(The | passes the list to tail, which keeps the last 10; Chapter 6 explains it.) Faster for an old command is reverse search: press Ctrl-RCtrl-R and type seqkit. The prompt changes to (reverse-i-search) and shows the newest command containing seqkit. Press Ctrl-RCtrl-R again for older matches, EnterEnter to run the one shown, or RightRight (or EscEsc) to put it on the line to edit first.
Editing a recalled line without the arrow keys (Table 5.13): jump to the start or end, move a word at a time, delete a word. The most useful one for this chapter’s habit is Alt-.Alt-., which inserts the last argument of the previous command. Preview with ls -d -- run2/*.tmp, then type rm -i -- and press Alt-.Alt-.: the same pattern appears, without retyping it.



Table 5.13: Keys for history and line editing.










Keys
Action
macOS note




UpUp / DownDown
earlier / later command



Ctrl-RCtrl-R
search history; again for older matches



Ctrl-ACtrl-A / Ctrl-ECtrl-E
start / end of the line



Alt-BAlt-B / Alt-FAlt-F
back / forward one word
needs Option as Meta (below)


Ctrl-WCtrl-W
delete the word before the cursor



Ctrl-UCtrl-U / Ctrl-KCtrl-K
delete to the start / to the end of the line



Alt-.Alt-.
insert the last argument of the previous command
needs Option as Meta


Ctrl-CCtrl-C
cancel the line, or stop a running program



Ctrl-DCtrl-D
end input; at an empty prompt, close the shell



Ctrl-LCtrl-L
clear the screen



TabTab
complete; twice to list choices







Ctrl-CCtrl-C stops a running program; stopping and managing programs properly (processes, Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z, kill) is Chapter 7. Ctrl-DCtrl-D at an empty prompt closes the shell: on a cluster that logs you out, so press it with care.
On a Mac, the AltAlt keys need the Option key to act as Meta: in Terminal, Settings → Profiles → Keyboard → Use Option as Meta key; in iTerm2, Settings → Profiles → Keys, Left Option key: Esc+. VS Code’s built-in terminal may keep some shortcuts for itself.
You may also see !! (run the previous command again) and !$ (its last argument) in other people’s notes. They run without showing you the command first, so this book does not use them.
Where history lives. Bash keeps it in ~/.bash_history. Each shell normally loads that file when it starts and saves its own commands when it exits, so a terminal that is already open will not show commands typed in another one, even after that one is closed; a new terminal will. Anything you type on the command line is stored there, so never put a password or a token in a command (Chapter 4). How much history is kept is a setting in ~/.bashrc (Chapter 7).






TipSearch, don’t scroll



Ctrl-RCtrl-R finds an old command by any part of it, and Alt-.Alt-. inserts the last argument of the previous one.



Check yourself. Name two ways to rerun yesterday’s seqkit stats command without retyping it.






TipAnswer





Press UpUp until it appears; or press Ctrl-RCtrl-R and type seqkit. (history | tail and copying also works.)

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.12 Summary

Before a program starts, bash reads the line into words (respecting quotes), expands ~, wildcards, and $… where quoting allows, removes the quotes, and starts the command with the resulting arguments. Builtins such as cd are part of bash; most commands are programs.
Paths are absolute (from / or ~) or relative (from the current working directory, which pwd prints), even inside a script. . is here, .. is up one, cd - goes back, cd goes home.
cp and mv overwrite silently and rm has no undo: preview with ls -d --, then use -i. A relative link target is read from the link’s own folder; remove links with unlink, no trailing slash.
An unquoted wildcard is matched by bash, each name one argument; no match passes the pattern on unchanged. Quote names with spaces, and quote patterns meant for the program, such as find -name "*.fq.gz". Tab completes names and catches typos. Lowercase names without spaces or special characters need none of this care.
find <where> <tests> finds files by name, type, depth, size, and age. head, tail, less, and file look inside files without loading them whole; zless reads compressed text. Ctrl-RCtrl-R and the editing keys bring back and fix earlier commands.




Table 5.14: The chapter’s commands on one page.









Task
Command




Where am I? Go somewhere
pwd, cd path, cd .., cd -, cd


List
ls, ls -lh, ls -a, ls -t, ls -d -- names


Make
mkdir -p a/b, touch file


Copy, move, rename
cp -i a b, cp -r dir dir2, mv -i old new


Delete
ls -d -- names first, then rm -i -- names; rmdir dir


Link
ln -s /absolute/target name, readlink name, unlink name


Show arguments
printf '<%s>\n' pattern


Find
find dir -type f -name "*.fastq.gz", find dir -xtype l


Look inside
head -n 5, tail -n 5, less -S, zless, file, tail -f


Recall
UpUp, Ctrl-RCtrl-R, Alt-.Alt-., history

title: 5  Shell basics
text:
5.13 Exercises

Exercise 1. Where am I? Starting from ~, reach ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw twice: once with one absolute path, once with relative steps (one folder per cd). Then, from data/raw and without cd, list data/meta and the reference folder through data/ref using relative paths. Record each command in NOTEBOOK.md.






TipAnswer





cd ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw (or the path written out from /); then cd, cd bioinf-computing, cd data, cd raw. From data/raw: ls ../meta and ls ../ref/ (the trailing slash lists the shared folder’s files through the link: checksums.md5  genes.gtf.gz genome.fa.gz  README.md).





Exercise 2. Predict the wildcard. Do this before Exercise 3, which changes the folder. In ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share, write down what each line prints, then run them:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
echo */*_R1*
echo run?/*
echo */*.f*q.gz
echo *.bam
echo .*
echo run[!1]/*







TipAnswer





Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp
run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
*.bam
.old_settings
run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz.tmp run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
Points to check: *_R1* also catches the .tmp copy; *.f*q.gz matches both .fastq.gz and .fq.gz but not .tmp, because the name must end in q.gz; */ searches one level of subfolders, including the one with spaces; *.bam matched nothing and came out unchanged; run? does not match Run 3 final, because case matters and ? is one character. The order follows your system’s sorting rules and may differ slightly.





Exercise 3. Tidy a lab share. You inherit share/ and want a clean folder of read files to work from, without moving or copying the originals.

From ~/bioinf-computing-ch05, use find to list every read file, both .fastq.gz and .fq.gz, including those in the folder with spaces.
Make ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq/ and, from inside it, link each read file there with an absolute target, renaming .fq.gz to .fastq.gz so all six names are consistent. Two links, given complete; adapt them for the other four:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/"Run 3 final"/sample_C_R1.fq.gz sample_C_R1.fastq.gz

(With . as the name, the link takes the target’s own name.)
In share, remove the broken link ref with unlink (no slash), and delete the leftover .tmp file: preview with ls -d -- run2/*.tmp, then rm -i -- run2/*.tmp.
Check, with these four commands (the | sort puts the lines in order; Chapter 6):


Terminal (laptop)

find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy -type l -printf '%f -> %l\n' | sort
find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy -xtype l
find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy -type f
find ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share \( -xtype l -o -name '*.tmp' \) -print

The first lists each link and its target (%f the link’s name, %l the stored target); the second lists broken links; the third, ordinary files that should not be in tidy; the fourth, a broken link or .tmp file left in share. Only the first should print anything.







TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05
find share -type f \( -name "*.fastq.gz" -o -name "*.fq.gz" \)
mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz .
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/"Run 3 final"/sample_C_R1.fq.gz sample_C_R1.fastq.gz
ln -s ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/"Run 3 final"/sample_C_R2.fq.gz sample_C_R2.fastq.gz
cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
unlink ref
ls -d -- run2/*.tmp
rm -i -- run2/*.tmp

The first check prints these six lines, with your own home folder in place of /home/you (compare everything after it):
sample_A_R1.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz
sample_A_R2.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1/sample_A_R2.fastq.gz
sample_B_R1.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R1.fastq.gz
sample_B_R2.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run2/sample_B_R2.fastq.gz
sample_C_R1.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R1.fq.gz
sample_C_R2.fastq.gz -> /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/Run 3 final/sample_C_R2.fq.gz
The other three print nothing. Six working links that all point to the same file would pass the second check but not the first, which is why the first lists every target. Read a link to be sure it works: gunzip -c sample_C_R1.fastq.gz | head -n 4 in tidy/fastq prints the first record, @C.1.
The most common mistake is a relative target, such as ln -s run1/sample_A_R1.fastq.gz ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/tidy/fastq/ run from share: the link stores run1/…, which is read from tidy/fastq/, and the second check lists it as broken. Remove it with unlink and make it again with the absolute path.





Exercise 4. Read a log without opening it. In ~/bioinf-computing, list the logs newest first with ls -t logs. Find the newest log of a run that finished: Chapter 4 made a run fail on purpose, and its log, probably the newest, has no finished: line. Check each candidate with tail -n 3. In the finished log, show the first 3 lines with head, then open it in less and use /finished to jump to the last line. Which seqkit version did the run use?






TipAnswer





The failed run’s log ends with the md5sum lines, with no finished:. A finished log ends like this (the book’s, from Chapter 3):
command:  seqkit stats -T data/raw/*.fastq.gz
output:   e1d81de77934f7ab7b44bf72b7520b32  results/read_counts.tsv
finished: 2026-11-17 12:24:53 -0600
The version is on the seqkit: line, in the first lines head -n 5 shows: seqkit v2.14.0 in the book’s log. If you have no log at all, read the book’s in Chapter 3 and rerun the script there when you can.





Exercise 5. Peek into compressed data. Run file on data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz and data/ref/genes.gtf.gz. Look at the first read with zless, and at the first two lines of the annotation with gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | head -n 2. The first column of a GTF line names the chromosome. Which chromosome does each of the two lines name? Note what you find in NOTEBOOK.md.






TipAnswer





file says gzip compressed data for both. The first GTF line names not_in_genome, and the second I:
not_in_genome   ensembl CDS 335 646 .   +   0   exon_number "1"; gene_biotype "protein_coding"; …
I   ensembl exon    335 649 .   +   .   exon_id "YAL069W.1"; exon_number "1"; …
(Lines shortened here at ….) The genome file has one sequence, I, so the first line describes a chromosome that is not in the genome. This is a test file, and an odd line like this one tests how tools cope; of the file’s 600 lines, all the others are on I. Looking at the start of a file is how you catch such things before a tool does. GTF is Chapter 17.





Exercise 6. History drill. Using only Ctrl-RCtrl-R and the editing keys, recall Exercise 4’s head command and change it to tail without retyping the log’s name.






TipAnswer





Ctrl-RCtrl-R, type head -n, then RightRight to edit; Ctrl-ACtrl-A to jump to the start, Alt-FAlt-F past head, Ctrl-WCtrl-W to delete it, type tail, EnterEnter. Other key sequences work as well; the point is not to retype the path.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.1 What this chapter does
Core. Work through it, with the exercises.
Most bioinformatics files are plain text with one record per line: sample sheets, annotation (GTF), tables of counts. FASTQ is text too, with one read per four lines in the book’s files. So a dozen small tools, each doing one job, answer most quick questions about these files when you join them with |: how many reads, how long, how many of each kind, which lines match. That is the whole “Unix philosophy” this chapter needs: small tools, joined together.
You have run pipes already. In Chapter 1 you typed gunzip -c … | wc -l and wrote a result with >; Chapter 3’s script ends in 2>&1 | tee "$log"; Chapter 5 used history | tail. This chapter explains each piece, so you can change those commands and write your own.
Commands run on your laptop, from the project folder. You only read the project’s files here. Everything you write goes to a scratch folder, ~/bioinf-computing-ch06, never into data/; the one exception is your notes in NOTEBOOK.md, as in earlier chapters. Make the scratch folder and go to the project:
Stay in ~/bioinf-computing for the whole chapter: pixi run finds the book’s environment from there, and the commands use paths such as data/raw/… that start from it. Every file the chapter writes is named with its full scratch path, ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/….
The outputs shown were captured with GNU grep 3.12, GNU sed 4.10, GNU Awk 5.4.1, GNU coreutils 9.11, GNU gzip 1.15, and seqkit 2.14.0, in the en_US.UTF-8 locale. Other versions give the same results except where a block says otherwise.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch06
cd ~/bioinf-computing

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.2 Pipes
Rerun two commands from Chapter 1, this time on the project’s copy of the file:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l

@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFBFFBFFFFFFF
@SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB
200000
Take the pipe apart. gunzip -c on its own decompresses the file and prints all 200,000 lines to the screen: do not run it alone, or you will watch reads scroll past for a while (stop it with Ctrl-CCtrl-C). head -n 8 on its own, with no file name, waits for you to type lines; press Ctrl-CCtrl-C to get the prompt back (stopping programs properly is Chapter 7). Joined by |, the first program’s output becomes the second one’s input, and you see only what you asked for.
Now name it. Every program has one standard input (stdin) and one standard output (stdout). By default stdin is your keyboard and stdout is your screen. The pipe | connects the stdout of the program on its left to the stdin of the program on its right. No file is written in between, and both programs run at the same time: head starts printing while gunzip is still working.
A pipe saves you an intermediate file, not all memory or disk use. sort, for example, must read all its input before it can print the first line, and for big inputs it writes temporary files of its own (where, on a cluster, is Chapter 10).
Programs that read stdin when you give them no file name are called filters: head, wc, sort, cut, grep, sed, awk, and gzip all are. That is what [FILE]... meant in the usage line of gzip in Chapter 4: with no file, it reads stdin.
Build a pipeline one step at a time. Ask a real question: how long are the reads? Start with the sequence lines, which in this file are line 2 of every 4, and look at the result before adding the next step:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | head -n 3

CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
GGAATAGTATATGTTGAGCAAGTGTGTTGATGTAGTATAGTAAGTCAAATCTAAATTTATATCCAACATATGAAGCTAGACCAATCAACTTTTGCATTTCA
Sequences only. Now print each length, sort the lengths, and count each value:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {print length($0)}' \
  | sort \
  | uniq -c

  50000 101
Every one of the 50,000 reads is 101 bases long. A long pipeline can be broken over lines with \ at the end of each line, one step per line, as here; it is still one command. Figure 6.1 shows what each step passes on, on a toy file of three reads.




  The pipeline gunzip -c reads.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | awk '{print length($0)}' | sort | uniq -c, run on a toy file of three reads, shown one program at a time with the lines that leave each one. Step 1: gunzip -c writes all 12 lines, four per read: @r1, ACGTTGCA, +, FFFFFFFF; @r2, GGATCC, +, FFFFFF; @r3, TTAGGCAT, +, FFFFFFFF. Step 2: awk keeps line 2 of every 4, the sequences ACGTTGCA, GGATCC, and TTAGGCAT. Step 3: a second awk prints each length: 8, 6, 8. Step 4: sort puts equal values together: 6, 8, 8. Step 5: uniq -c counts each run of equal lines: 1 6 and 2 8, one read of 6 bases and two of 8. On the book's real file the same pipeline prints 50000 101. Each pipe hands lines straight to the next program; no file is written in between.
  gunzip -c decompresses the file and writes all 12 lines, four per read.
  awk keeps line 2 of every 4: the sequences. This works only because the file has exactly four lines per read.
  A second awk prints the length of each sequence.
  sort puts equal values next to each other.
  uniq -c counts each run of equal lines: one read of 6 bases, two of 8. On the book's real file the same pipeline prints 50000 101.
  
    
      
    
    
      
    
  
  
  
  TERMINAL
  
    gunzip -c reads.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' |
    awk '{print length($0)}' | sort | uniq -c

    no file is written in between.
  




Figure 6.1: The read-length pipeline on a toy file of three reads, one program at a time. Each step prints lines that the next step reads; no file is written in between. (In the chapter’s command the two awk steps are one awk.) Use Next to step through.



awk 'NR % 4 == 2' means “print line 2, 6, 10, …”: NR is the line number and % the remainder after division. Section 6.8 explains awk. For now, note the assumption: this works because this file has exactly four lines per read, as you checked in Chapter 1. FASTQ in general does not promise that (Chapter 15), which is why format-aware tools exist (Section 6.10).
Two more things are worth knowing now. First, head stops reading after 8 lines, so gunzip is stopped too, before it reaches the end of the file. That is normal. Bash records each program’s exit status in the array PIPESTATUS:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8 > /dev/null
echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"

141 0
141 means gunzip was stopped because nobody was reading any more; 0 is head’s success. (> /dev/null throws the output away; Section 6.4.) The exact number can vary with the program and the timing. It matters in scripts that stop on any error (set -o pipefail, Chapter 8). Second, because it stops early, gunzip -c … | head says nothing about whether the rest of the file is intact. Checking the whole file is gzip -t, from Chapter 1.






ImportantKey idea



A pipe | joins one program’s standard output to the next program’s standard input. Build pipelines one step at a time, and look at the output after each step before adding the next.



Check yourself. What does gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 4 | wc -l print?






TipAnswer





4. wc counts only the four lines head passed on; it never sees the rest of the file.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.3 Redirection and the > trap
Chapter 1 saved a read count with > and added the second file’s count with >>. Do the same into the scratch folder, running the > line twice:


Terminal (laptop)

echo "SRR6357070_1 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
echo "SRR6357070_1 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt

SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000
One line: the second > replaced the first. Now the R2 line, with >>, also twice:


Terminal (laptop)

echo "SRR6357070_2 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" >> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
echo "SRR6357070_2 reads: $(( $(gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | wc -l) / 4 ))" >> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt

SRR6357070_1 reads: 50000
SRR6357070_2 reads: 50000
SRR6357070_2 reads: 50000
>> adds to the end every time, so the R2 line is there twice. Rerunning a command that appends is a common way to get duplicated rows. > replaces a file’s contents; >> appends. Both create the file if it does not exist.
< goes the other way: it connects a file to a program’s stdin.


Terminal (laptop)

wc -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
wc -l < ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt

3 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/fastq_summary.txt
3
Given a file name, wc prints the name too; reading stdin, it has no name to print. That makes < handy when you want only the number.

6.3.1 The trap: cmd file > file
Make a three-line toy file and try to sort it “in place”:


Terminal (laptop)

printf 'b\na\nc\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
sort ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
wc -c ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt

b
a
c
0 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
Zero bytes: the file is empty, with no error and no warning. The reason is the order of events (Figure 6.2). Bash sets up the redirection before it starts the program, and setting up > opens the file for writing, which empties it. Only then does sort start, read the now empty toy.txt, and write nothing. The same happens with grep, cut, awk, and any other command whose input and > output are the same file.




  Why sort toy.txt > toy.txt leaves an empty file, and the safe route. Step 1: the shell opens toy.txt for writing and empties it before sort starts, so the lines b, a, c are gone. Step 2: sort starts, reads the now-empty toy.txt, and writes nothing, leaving toy.txt at 0 bytes. Safe route: write a new file with sort toy.txt > toy.sorted.txt, check it with cat toy.sorted.txt, which shows a, b, c, then replace the original with mv toy.sorted.txt toy.txt. Chapter 3's script did the same with read_counts.tsv.tmp.
  
    
      
    
  
  
  
  YOU TYPE
  sort toy.txt > toy.txt
  same file on both sides
  
  
  
  1
  
    The shell opens toy.txt for writing
    and empties it, before sort starts.
  
  toy.txt
  
  
    b
    a
    c
  
  before
  >
  
  toy.txt
  
  
    b
    a
    c
  
  
    
    
    
  
  ✗ emptied
  
  
  
  2
  
    sort starts, reads the now-empty
    toy.txt, and writes nothing.
  
  toy.txt
  
  empty
  
  
  sort
  0 lines in
  
  toy.txt
  
  ✗ 0 bytes
  
  
  ✓ Safe: write a new file, check it, then mv
  
    
    
    
    1
    2
    3
  
  
  
  
  
    sort toy.txt > toy.sorted.txt
    cat toy.sorted.txt
    mv toy.sorted.txt toy.txt
  
  
    a new file; toy.txt is untouched
    ✓ check: it shows a, b, c in order
    replace the original only after the check
  
  Chapter 3's script did the same with read_counts.tsv.tmp.




Figure 6.2: Why sort toy.txt > toy.txt leaves an empty file. The shell empties toy.txt before sort starts, so sort reads nothing. The safe route: write a new file, check it, then mv it over the old one.



The fix is the route in the figure: write to a new name, check it, then move it into place.


Terminal (laptop)

printf 'b\na\nc\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt
sort ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.sorted.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.sorted.txt
mv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.sorted.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt

a
b
c
This is exactly what Chapter 3’s script does: seqkit writes results/read_counts.tsv.tmp, and only after that succeeds does mv put it in place of read_counts.tsv. Now you can see why.






WarningPitfall: cmd file > file empties the file



The shell empties the output file before the command reads it. Write to a new name, check the result, then mv it over the original.








CautionMisconception: “sort data.txt > data.txt sorts the file in place”



Reality. The shell empties data.txt before sort starts, so you are left with an empty file. Redirection never edits a file in place.


A safety net: noclobber. Chapter 5 showed cp -n, which refuses to overwrite. Bash has the same idea for >. Try it inside ( … ), which runs the commands in a separate copy of the shell, so the setting goes away afterwards:


Terminal (laptop)

( set -o noclobber; echo x > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt )
echo $?

bash: /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.txt: cannot overwrite existing file
1
With noclobber on, > refuses to replace an existing file, and >| forces it. It guards > only: >>, tee, cp, mv, and sed -i still overwrite. You could turn it on for good in your ~/.bashrc (Chapter 7), but this book does not, because later chapters overwrite files on purpose. The habits that protect you are the .tmp-then-mv route and Chapter 3’s read-only data/raw/:


Terminal (laptop)

echo test > data/raw/notes.txt

bash: data/raw/notes.txt: Permission denied
The same message stops sort data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz > data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz before it can empty the file. (What permissions are is Chapter 7.) Note the two quieter dangers of >: on a mistyped name it silently makes a new file, and on the right name it silently replaces the old contents.


6.3.2 tee: save and see
Sometimes you want a result in a file and on the screen. tee copies its stdin to a file and to its stdout:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats -T \
  data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz \
  | tee ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv \
  | cut -f1,4

file    num_seqs
data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz  50000
data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz  50000
The full eight-column table went into counts.tsv, and the screen shows only columns 1 and 4 (cut, Section 6.5). -T makes seqkit print a tab-separated table, which cut needs; seqkit’s default table is laid out for people to read. You will also see a processed files line, which the next section explains. tee -a appends instead of replacing; Chapter 3’s script used tee "$log" to save its messages while showing them.



Table 6.1: Redirection operators. cmd is any command.











Operator
What it does
Example
Danger




\|
stdout of the left command to stdin of the right
gunzip -c f.gz \| wc -l
the left command’s errors still reach the screen


>
stdout to a file, replacing it
cmd > out.txt
empties the file first, even if it is the input


>>
stdout to the end of a file
cmd >> log.txt
rerunning duplicates lines


<
a file to stdin
wc -l < f.txt



2>
stderr to a file
cmd 2> err.txt



2>&1
stderr to wherever stdout goes now
cmd > all.txt 2>&1
order matters (Section 6.4)


&>
both streams to a file (bash)
cmd &> all.txt
results and messages mixed


>\|
> even when noclobber is on
cmd >\| out.txt



tee f
stdin to a file and to stdout
cmd \| tee out.txt
replaces f; tee -a appends


/dev/null
a file that discards everything
cmd 2> /dev/null
hides messages you may need







Check yourself. You run grep -v '^#' notes.txt > notes.txt. What is in notes.txt now?






TipAnswer





Nothing. The shell emptied notes.txt before grep started, so grep read an empty file. Write to notes.clean.txt, check it, then mv.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.4 Standard output and standard error
Send the seqkit table into a file:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats -T data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv

processed files:  2 / 2 [======] ETA: 0s. done
The table went into counts.tsv, but a line still appeared on the screen. If > sends “the output” to a file, where did this line come from?
Two output streams. Every program has a second output, standard error (stderr). By convention, programs write their results to stdout and their messages, progress, warnings, and errors to stderr. Both go to your terminal by default, so they look the same until you redirect one of them (Figure 6.3). > and | carry stdout only; stderr still reaches the screen. seqkit’s progress line is on stderr, which is why it stayed. (On screen it updates itself in place; saved to a file, it shows the cursor codes it uses for that. Chapter 3’s script runs seqkit stats --quiet, which turns the line off.)




  Standard output and standard error in three cases: default, redirected to a file, and through a pipe. Each program has one input, stdin, and two outputs: stdout (solid arrow) and stderr (dashed arrow). Top, seqkit stats -T run with no redirection: stdout, the table, and stderr, the progress line processed files: 2 / 2 done, both go to the terminal. Middle, seqkit stats -T with > counts.tsv: only stdout goes to the file counts.tsv; stderr still reaches the terminal, which shows only the progress line. Bottom, gunzip -c broken.fastq.gz | wc -l: only gunzip's stdout enters the pipe and becomes the stdin of wc; gunzip's stderr skips the pipe and prints gzip: broken.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file on the terminal; wc then prints 89515, a partial count of lines, not a read count.
  
    
      
    
    
      
    
    
      
    
  
  
  
  1 · Default: both streams go to the terminal
  you ran seqkit stats -T …
  
  stdin
  
  seqkit stats
  
  stdout
  
  stderr
  
  TERMINAL
  
    file  format  type  num_seqs …
    …     FASTQ   DNA   50000    …
    processed files: 2 / 2 … done
  
  
  
  2 · > file: only stdout goes to the file
  you ran seqkit stats -T … > counts.tsv
  
  stdin
  
  seqkit stats
  
  stdout
  > counts.tsv
  
  stderr
  
  
  
  counts.tsv
  file: the table
  
  TERMINAL
  processed files: 2 / 2 … done
  
  
  3 · cmd1 | cmd2: only stdout enters the pipe
  you ran gunzip -c broken.fastq.gz | wc -l
  
  stdin
  
  gunzip -c
  
  stdout
  through |, becomes stdin of wc
  
  wc -l
  
  
  stderr: skips the pipe
  
  stdout
  
  TERMINAL
  
    gzip: broken.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file
    89515
  
  ← partial count: not a read count




Figure 6.3: A program has one input (stdin) and two outputs: stdout for results and stderr for messages. By default both reach the terminal. > file moves only stdout; a pipe carries only stdout, so the error from gunzip skips wc and goes straight to the screen.



To send stderr somewhere, put its number in front of >. Stdin is stream 0, stdout 1, and stderr 2, so 2> redirects stderr. Go back to Chapter 4’s truncated file. Make a copy in the scratch folder and run seqkit on it, with each stream to its own file:


Terminal (laptop)

head -c 1000000 data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz \
  > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/out.tsv \
  2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/err.txt
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/out.tsv
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/err.txt

file    format  type    num_seqs    sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
[ERRO] /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF
[ERRO]
The header row (a result) is in out.tsv; the error is in err.txt. Nothing reached the screen. cat shows [ERRO] in red, as seqkit printed it. cat -A, which shows every invisible character, reveals how:


Terminal (laptop)

cat -A ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/err.txt

^[[31m[ERRO]^[[0m /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected EOF$
^[[31m[ERRO]^[[0m $
^[[31m and ^[[0m are colour codes: “red on”, “colour off”. $ marks each line’s end. Colour codes end up in log files this way; they are harmless, but they are why a log can look odd in an editor. (cat -A returns in Section 6.5 for tabs, and Chapter 7 uses it for Windows line endings.)
Both streams into one file. 2>&1 means “send stderr to wherever stdout is going now”. So the order matters:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz \
  > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/both.txt 2>&1

puts both streams in both.txt. Written the other way round, 2>&1 > both.txt, stderr is pointed at the screen (where stdout was at that moment) and only stdout goes to the file. Bash’s shorthand &> does the first version. Use these for logs, never for results: a results table with error lines in it breaks the next tool that reads it. Chapter 3’s script wrapped its commands in { … }, then sent 2>&1 | tee "$log", so its log keeps the messages from both streams, while the results went to their own file with >.
/dev/null is a special file that discards whatever is written to it. 2> /dev/null hides messages. Use it only for messages you have read and know you do not need, such as seqkit’s progress line; never to make a screen of errors look clean.
The pipe carries stdout only. Count the lines of the broken file:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz | wc -l
echo $?


gzip: /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz: unexpected end of file
89515
0
Read this carefully. Decompression failed partway, after producing some text. The error went to stderr, around the pipe, to your screen. wc successfully counted the text it received: 89,515 lines. That count is incomplete and cannot be used as a read count. And echo $? says 0, because a pipeline’s exit status is the status of its last command, wc, which did its job. "${PIPESTATUS[@]}" here would show 1 0: gunzip failed, wc succeeded. (The exact count depends on the gzip version: Apple’s gzip on a Mac stopped at 89,253. Either way, it is partial.)
Do not try to spot damage by checking whether a line count divides by 4: another cut could land on a multiple of 4 and still be wrong. Know your expected count (50,000 reads here), and read the messages. set -o pipefail (Chapter 8) makes a pipeline fail when any stage reports failure, but it cannot help when a tool reports success despite an error, as seqkit 2.14.0 did in Chapter 4. That is why the result checks from Chapter 4 still matter.






ImportantKey idea



By convention, results go to stdout and messages to stderr. > and | carry only stdout, so errors still reach the screen, and a pipeline can “succeed” on broken input. This is a convention tools follow, not a rule the shell enforces: some tools mix the two or write their own log files.



Check yourself. A command prints a table and some warnings. You want the table in out.tsv and the warnings in run.log. Write the redirection. And after seqkit stats … > counts.tsv, why was a progress line still on the screen?






TipAnswer





cmd > out.tsv 2> run.log. The progress line is on stderr, and > redirects only stdout.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
section: 6.5 Counting and summarising: wc, cut, sort, uniq
text:
6.5 Counting and summarising: wc, cut, sort, uniq
Start with a table small enough to check by eye: the practice sample table from Chapter 5. If you built Chapter 5’s practice folder, it is ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples.tsv. Either way, make the chapter’s own copy with this block (the same lines Chapter 5 used; the list and printf are explained in Chapter 8):


Terminal (laptop)

rows=(sample run_folder condition reads
  sample_C "Run 3 final" treated 12
  sample_A run1 control 9
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_E run5 treated 105
  sample_B run2 control 30
  sample_D run4 control 8)
printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' "${rows[@]}" > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
md5sum ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv

971d8f742cb76a8d181d3bdc3dcbceaa  /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
If you have Chapter 5’s file, md5sum on it gives the same checksum. From here on the chapter uses the copy in ~/bioinf-computing-ch06. (It is not the project’s data/meta/samples.tsv, which has different columns.) Look at it:


Terminal (laptop)

cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
wc -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
cat -A ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | head -n 3

sample  run_folder  condition   reads
sample_C    Run 3 final treated 12
sample_A    run1    control 9
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_E    run5    treated 105
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_D    run4    control 8
7 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
sample^Irun_folder^Icondition^Ireads$
sample_C^IRun 3 final^Itreated^I12$
sample_A^Irun1^Icontrol^I9$
A header and six rows, separated by tabs (cat -A shows each tab as ^I). By eye: sample_B is listed twice, on rows 3 and 5. Can the tools find that?
uniq only merges neighbours. cut -f1 takes column 1; uniq -c counts repeated lines:


Terminal (laptop)

cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | uniq -c

      1 sample
      1 sample_C
      1 sample_A
      1 sample_B
      1 sample_E
      1 sample_B
      1 sample_D
sample_B appears twice, each with count 1. uniq compares each line only with the line before it, and the two sample_B lines are not next to each other. Sort first, so equal values become neighbours:


Terminal (laptop)

cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort | uniq -c
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort | uniq -d

      1 sample
      1 sample_A
      2 sample_B
      1 sample_C
      1 sample_D
      1 sample_E
sample_B
2 sample_B. uniq -d prints only the lines that occur more than once. sort | uniq -c is the habit: it counts equal values wherever they sit in the file.






CautionMisconception: “uniq removes or counts all duplicate lines”



Reality. uniq only merges identical lines that are next to each other. Sort first: sort | uniq -c.


Skip the header. Count the conditions:


Terminal (laptop)

cut -f3 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort | uniq -c
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c

      1 condition
      4 control
      2 treated
      4 control
      2 treated
The first version counted the header as a value. tail -n +2 prints from line 2 onwards, which drops it. (tail -n 2, without the +, would print the last two lines.)
Numbers sort as text. Sort the rows by the reads column, as text and then as numbers:


Terminal (laptop)

tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -t$'\t' -k4,4
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n

sample_E    run5    treated 105
sample_C    Run 3 final treated 12
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_D    run4    control 8
sample_A    run1    control 9
sample_D    run4    control 8
sample_A    run1    control 9
sample_C    Run 3 final treated 12
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_E    run5    treated 105
As text, 105 comes first, because sort compares character by character and 1 comes before 3, 8, and 9. With n, the column is compared as numbers: 8, 9, 12, 30, 30, 105. The pieces: -t$'\t' says the fields are separated by tabs ($'\t' is how you type a tab character in bash); -k4,4 sorts on field 4 only, from field 4 to field 4; the n after it makes that key numeric.
The duplicate matters. sort -u keeps one copy of each identical line:


Terminal (laptop)

tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -u

sample_A    run1    control 9
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_C    Run 3 final treated 12
sample_D    run4    control 8
sample_E    run5    treated 105
Five samples. The header was removed with tail -n +2 before sorting, so it cannot end up among the data. The reads column adds up to 194 with the duplicate and 164 without it (you will compute both with awk in Section 6.8): a duplicated metadata row inflates totals silently. sort -u removes only rows that are identical in every column. Two rows with the same sample name and different values are a conflict to resolve, not a duplicate to drop (Chapter 14). Note also that sample_D and sample_E have no read files in Chapter 5’s practice folder: a sample table and the files on disk can disagree, which Chapter 14 checks properly.

6.5.1 The real sample sheet
Chapter 3 saved nf-core’s sample sheet unchanged as data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv. It is comma-separated, so tell cut the delimiter with -d,:


Terminal (laptop)

cut -d, -f1 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | sort | uniq -c

      1 RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1
      1 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1
      2 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
      1 sample
      2 WT_REP1
      1 WT_REP2
Seven runs under five test labels: WT_REP1 and RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2 each group two runs, so the test exercises merging (they are not one sample sequenced twice; Section 3.7 checked them against the archive). The header sample is counted too; tail -n +2 removes it. Here the repeated labels already sit next to each other in the file, so uniq -c alone would happen to give the same counts. The practice table is why you sort anyway. One more column, the strandedness setting:


Terminal (laptop)

tail -n +2 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | cut -d, -f4 | sort | uniq -c

      2 auto
      5 reverse
Sort order depends on the locale. Look again at where sample landed above: between the RAP1_… and WT_… names. Now sort with LC_ALL=C:


Terminal (laptop)

cut -d, -f1 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | LC_ALL=C sort | uniq -c

      1 RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1
      1 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1
      2 RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
      2 WT_REP1
      1 WT_REP2
      1 sample
Same counts, different order. Your locale (language settings) tells sort how to order letters. In en_US.UTF-8, upper and lower case are mixed together, as in a dictionary. In the C locale, characters are ordered by their byte values, so all capitals come before all lower-case letters. LC_ALL=C in front of a command sets it for that command only. Use it when the order must be the same on every computer. Tools that compare sorted files, such as join and comm, need their input sorted by the same rules they use themselves; if you sort with LC_ALL=C, run them with LC_ALL=C too. Which locale you have by default depends on the system: WSL’s Ubuntu uses C.UTF-8, which already sorts like C, so there both commands give this second order. Your settings are Chapter 7.






TipSort before you count



Sort before uniq -c, so equal values are counted wherever they are in the file. Use LC_ALL=C sort when the order must be reproducible.




6.5.2 The annotation
Now the yeast annotation, data/ref/genes.gtf.gz, read through the data/ref link. A GTF file has nine tab-separated columns, and column 3 is the feature type. Count the types, most common first:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr

    129 exon
    124 transcript
    118 CDS
    115 start_codon
    114 stop_codon
The final sort -k1,1nr, piece by piece: sort on field 1 (the counts), as numbers (n), in reverse (r), largest first. With no -t, sort splits fields at blanks, and the leading spaces from uniq -c are skipped. What is missing is a finding too: there are no gene lines. Many GTF files have one per gene; this test file has transcripts, exons, coding parts (CDS), and start and stop codons only, 600 lines in all. A tool that expects gene lines would find none here.
Now column 1, the sequence (chromosome) names:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c
gunzip -c data/ref/genome.fa.gz | grep '^>'

    599 I
      1 not_in_genome
>I
You may remember the not_in_genome line from Exercise 5 of Chapter 5, where it was the first line of the file. Counting shows that it is the only one: 599 lines are on chromosome I, the one sequence in the genome (the grep prints FASTA header lines, which start with >; Section 6.6). nf-core put that line there on purpose, to test that the pipeline copes with an annotation line on a sequence the genome does not have (nf-core/test-datasets commit 1b17b24, “Add gtf line using chromosome not in genome”). Real annotations and genomes do not always match either (Chapter 15). Two minutes of counting found something you would otherwise meet as a pipeline error.
Text sort vs numeric sort, on real coordinates. Column 4 holds start positions. Take the first 12 transcript starts and sort them both ways:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | grep -w transcript | cut -f4 | head -n 12 \
  > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/starts.txt
sort ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/starts.txt | tr '\n' ' '; echo
sort -n ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/starts.txt | tr '\n' ' '; echo

10091 11565 12046 13363 1807 21566 22395 24000 2480 335 538 7235
335 538 1807 2480 7235 10091 11565 12046 13363 21566 22395 24000
Text order puts 10091 before 1807 and 335 near the end. (tr '\n' ' ' turns newlines into spaces, so the list fits on one line; echo ends the line.) Sorting coordinates as text is a classic way to break interval files (Chapter 17).






CautionMisconception: “sort puts numbers in numeric order”



Reality. By default sort compares text, character by character, so 10091 comes before 1807. Use sort -n, with -k to choose the column.


One more count, on the reads. How many distinct sequences are there among R1’s 50,000 reads, and which is most common?


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | sort -u | wc -l
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr | head -n 3 | cut -c1-40

21662
    208 GTTAGGAGTGTGCAATACCTTTATTGATGTTT
    186 CTTTGACCCAGGTAGGTAGGAATTGAGAGGGA
    123 CTTTAAATGGGTCAGGGAATTCGGTAGGAGAT
21,662 distinct sequences; the most common one appears 208 times. (cut -c1-40 keeps the first 40 characters of each line, to fit.) What duplicated reads mean for an RNA-seq experiment is a quality-control question for the Genomics and Transcriptomics books; here, the point is that the same sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr pattern answered it.

Check yourself. cut -d, -f1 samplesheet_upstream.csv | uniq -c gives the right counts, but cut -f1 samples.tsv | uniq -c on the practice table does not. Why?






TipAnswer





In the sample sheet the repeated labels are on neighbouring lines; in the practice table the two sample_B rows are not, and uniq only merges neighbours. Sort first.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.6 Finding lines: grep
grep prints the lines that match a pattern. With -c it counts them. Count the read headers in both mate files:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c '^@SRR'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | grep -c '^@SRR'

50000
50000
^ means “at the start of the line” (Section 6.7). Now a real question from Chapter 4: the paper’s methods trimmed the adapter AGATCGGAAGAGC with cutadapt. How many reads contain that exact sequence? Search the sequence lines only:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | grep -c AGATCGGAAGAGC
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | grep -c AGATCGGAAGAGC

1916
1910
1,916 reads in R1 and 1,910 in R2 contain this exact 13-letter motif. That is not a measure of adapter contamination: partial adapters at a read’s end and adapters with a sequencing error are missed. Trimming tools and quality reports measure that properly (the applied books). Note what -c counts: matching lines. A line with the motif twice counts once; grep -o prints each match on its own line, if you want to count occurrences.
A gene in the annotation:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | grep -w 'gene_name "CDC19"' | cut -f1-8

I   ensembl CDS 71786   73285   .   +   0
I   ensembl exon    71786   73288   .   +   .
I   ensembl start_codon 71786   71788   .   +   0
I   ensembl transcript  71786   73288   .   +   .
I   ensembl stop_codon  73286   73288   .   +   0
Five lines for CDC19 (pyruvate kinase), on the + strand from 71,786 to 73,288. -w matches whole words only, so a search for CDC1 would not match CDC19. The pattern is in single quotes because it contains spaces and double quotes (Chapter 5).

6.6.1 The @ trap
Would grep -c '^@' also count the reads? On this file, yes:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c '^@'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 0' | grep -o . | sort | uniq -c

50000
 216720 /
    280 #
 191521 <
  11539 7
 486514 B
4143426 F
The second command lists every character used in the quality lines (line 4 of every 4; grep -o . prints each character on its own line). This file uses only six quality characters, and @ is not one of them. But @ is a valid quality character (a base quality of 31, Chapter 15), so in other files a quality line can start with @. Here is a two-read toy file where one does:


Terminal (laptop)

printf '@r1\nACGT\n+\n@III\n@r2\nTTGA\n+\nIIII\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq
grep -c '^@' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq
awk 'NR % 4 == 1' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq | wc -l
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq

3
2
file    format  type    num_seqs    sum_len min_len avg_len max_len
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/at_quality.fastq    FASTQ   DNA 2   8   4   4.0 4
Two reads; grep says 3. Counting header lines by position (awk 'NR % 4 == 1') gets 2, but only because the file has four lines per read, and it checks nothing else. seqkit reads the format and gets 2 with no assumption. That is the same lesson as Chapter 1: true for this file is not true for FASTQ.






WarningPitfall: grep -c '^@' is not a read count



@ is also a quality character, so a quality line can start with it. Count by position in a file you know has four lines per read, or, in general, with pixi run seqkit stats.




6.6.2 Flags you will use
To see a whole read around a match, -A 3 prints 3 lines after each matching line:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -A 3 '^@SRR6357070\.6710070 '

@SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
+
BBBBBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB
The backslash before the dot and the space at the end make the pattern exact; the next section explains both. When nothing matches, grep prints nothing (or 0 with -c) and returns exit status 1:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c ZZZZ
echo $?

0
1
Status 1 means “no match”, not “error” (an error is 2). That matters in scripts that stop on any nonzero status (Chapter 8).

Check yourself. gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c CTG gives 35,761. Is that the number of reads containing CTG?






TipAnswer





Here, yes, but only because this file’s quality lines use none of the letters C, T, G. In general, search the sequence lines only: awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | grep -c CTG. Both give 35,761 on this file.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.7 Regular expressions
Count an EcoRI restriction site, GAATTC, in R1, then the same pattern with one letter replaced by a dot:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c GAATTC
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -c 'GA.TTC'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | grep -o 'GA.TTC' | sort | uniq -c

2818
11404
   2901 GAATTC
   2917 GACTTC
   2483 GAGTTC
      1 GANTTC
   4083 GATTTC
Four times as many lines. In a grep pattern, . matches any one character, and grep -o shows what it matched: A, C, G, T, and once an N. (-o counts matches, so its numbers add up to more than the 2,818 matching lines.) The pattern is a regular expression, or regex: a small language for describing text.
Two more on the sample sheet. List the run IDs, then count the FASTQ file names:


Terminal (laptop)

grep -o 'SRR[0-9]*_1' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | sed 's/_1$//'
grep -Eo 'SRR[0-9]+_[12]\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | wc -l

SRR6357070
SRR6357071

Seven runs, and 11 file names: four runs with two files each, plus three runs that this test sheet uses as single-end, with one. (sed 's/_1$//' removes the _1 at the end; Section 6.8.) Figure 6.4 takes the second pattern apart.




  The parts of the regular expression SRR[0-9]+_[12]\.fastq\.gz, and three strings tested against it. SRR, the underscore, fastq, and gz are literal characters. [0-9] matches one character from a class: any digit. The plus sign means one or more of the previous item, in grep -E. [12] matches one character: 1 or 2. Each \. is an escaped dot that matches a real dot. SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz matches. SRR6357070_3.fastq.gz does not match, because 3 is not in [12]. SRR6357070_1.fastqXgz does not match, because \. needs a real dot; without the backslash, the dot would match the X.

Figure 6.4: The parts of SRR[0-9]+_[12]\.fastq\.gz, and three strings tested against it. Only the first matches: 3 is not in [12], and \. needs a real dot.



Now name the parts. Most characters match themselves (literals). A few have special meanings (Table 6.4):

. matches any one character; \. matches a real dot. The backslash turns a special character back into a literal.
[0-9] matches one character from a class, here any digit; [12] matches 1 or 2; [^ACGT] matches any character except those listed.
* means “zero or more of the item before it”, + “one or more”, ? “zero or one”, and {10,} “10 or more”.
^ and $ anchor the match to the start and end of the line.
( ) groups, and | means “or”: ^(WT|RAP1_IAA) matches lines that start with either.

Basic and extended syntax. grep and sed use basic regular expressions by default, where +, ?, { }, ( ), and | are ordinary characters unless you put a backslash before them. grep -E, sed -E, and awk use extended syntax, where they are special without one. So the same pattern behaves differently:


Terminal (laptop)

grep -c 'SRR[0-9]+_' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
grep -Ec 'SRR[0-9]+_' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv

0
7
In basic syntax, + was a literal plus sign, and no line contains one. This book uses -E whenever a pattern needs +, ?, |, or groups. (GNU grep -P adds Perl-style patterns; you will meet it in other people’s commands.) Always put a regex in single quotes, so bash does not treat *, ?, [ ], or $ as its own special characters first.

6.7.1 Try patterns
Figure 6.5 runs a pattern against eight fixed lines from the book’s files. Pick one of the examples from the list, or type your own. Change one character at a time and watch what matches: try GAATTC, then GA.TTC; fastq.gz, then fastq\.gz; reverse$, then reverse.

viewof pattern = Inputs.text({
  label: "Pattern",
  value: "GA.TTC",
  placeholder: "type a regular expression",
  datalist: [
    "GAATTC", "GA.TTC", "^@SRR", "SRR[0-9]+_2\\.fastq\\.gz",
    "reverse$", "^(WT|RAP1_IAA)", "fastq.gz", "^[ACGT]+$"
  ],
  spellcheck: false
})










testerLines = [
  "sample,fastq_1,fastq_2,strandedness",
  "WT_REP1,SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz,SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz,auto",
  "RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1,SRR6357073_1.fastq.gz,,reverse",
  "RAP1_IAA_30M_REP1,SRR6357076_1.fastq.gz,SRR6357076_2.fastq.gz,reverse",
  "@SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932",
  "GTCAGACAACAACTTTTGGACCTTTGGAATTCTGGTAGAACC",
  "+",
  "BBBBBFFFFFFFBFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB"
]

testerResult = {
  if (pattern === "") return {error: "Type a pattern.", rows: []};
  let re;
  try { re = new RegExp(pattern, "g"); }
  catch (e) { return {error: "Not a valid pattern: " + e.message, rows: []}; }
  const rows = testerLines.map((line) => {
    const parts = [];
    let last = 0, any = false;
    for (const m of line.matchAll(re)) {
      any = true;
      if (m[0].length === 0) continue;
      parts.push({text: line.slice(last, m.index), hit: false});
      parts.push({text: m[0], hit: true});
      last = m.index + m[0].length;
    }
    parts.push({text: line.slice(last), hit: false});
    return {line, parts, any};
  });
  return {error: null, rows};
}

{
  const lh = 22, top = 30, h = top + testerLines.length * lh + 30;
  const n = testerResult.rows.filter((r) => r.any).length;
  return htl.svg`<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 720 ${h}" role="img"
      aria-label="${testerResult.error ?? `${n} of 8 lines match the pattern ${pattern}`}">
    <text x="8" y="18" font-size="13" class="fill-muted">${
      testerResult.error ?? `${n} of 8 lines match`}</text>
    ${testerResult.rows.map((r, i) => htl.svg`<g>
      <text x="8" y=${top + 14 + i * lh} font-size="13"
            class=${r.any ? "fill-given" : "fill-muted"}>${r.any ? "match" : "—"}</text>
      <text x="64" y=${top + 14 + i * lh} font-size="12.5" class="mono">${
        r.parts.map((p) => p.hit
          ? htl.svg`<tspan class="fill-given" font-weight="700" text-decoration="underline">${p.text}</tspan>`
          : htl.svg`<tspan class=${r.any ? "" : "fill-muted"}>${p.text}</tspan>`)
      }</text>
    </g>`)}
  </svg>`;
}

Engines differ in details. GNU grep -Eo 'a|ab' on the text ab prints ab (the longest match), while JavaScript’s /a|ab/ picks a (the first alternative that fits). The tester’s examples avoid such cases.


6.7.2 Globs are not regular expressions
Chapter 5 promised this. A wildcard (glob) and a regex can look alike and mean different things:


Terminal (laptop)

grep -c '*.fastq.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
grep -c '.*\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv
grep -o '[^/]*\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | head -n 3

0
7
SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz
*.fastq.gz as a glob means “any name ending in .fastq.gz”. As a regex it means something else: a * at the very start has nothing before it to repeat, so grep reads it as a literal *, then any character, then fastq, any character, gz. No line contains a *, so 0. In a regex, “anything” is .* and a real dot is \.: .*\.fastq\.gz matches the 7 data rows. The third line prints the file names themselves: [^/]* is “any run of characters that are not /”, so the match starts after the last / of each URL. (In a regex, “ends in .fastq.gz” would be \.fastq\.gz$; no line of this sheet ends that way, because each row ends with its strandedness.)

Characters

In a regex (grep, sed, awk, R, Python)
Example

any one character

glob {R1,R2}; regex A{10,}












CautionMisconception: “* means the same in grep as in ls”



Reality. In a glob, * is “any characters”. In a regex, * is “zero or more of the previous character”, and . is “any character”. The regex for “anything” is .*.


The same regexes in R and Python. Simple patterns like ^SRR[0-9]+ work the same in R, grepl("^SRR[0-9]+", x) (base R uses extended syntax), and in Python, re.search(r"^SRR[0-9]+", s). But they are separate engines, not one universal regex: base R, R’s stringr package, Python’s re, JavaScript, and GNU grep differ in details such as backslashes (R needs "\\." inside a string; Python’s raw strings r"\." avoid that) and which alternative wins in a|ab. Chapter 12 and Chapter 13 use them. One warning for all languages: regexes for structured formats, such as quoted CSV fields or GTF attributes, get fragile fast; use a parser for those.

Check yourself. Does grep 'fastq.gz' match the text fastqXgz?






TipAnswer





Yes: . matches any character, including X. Use 'fastq\.gz', or grep -F 'fastq.gz', which treats the whole pattern as plain text.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
section: 6.8 Editing streams with sed, computing with awk
text:
6.8 Editing streams with sed, computing with awk

6.8.1 sed: substitute
Chromosome names differ between sources: chr1 in one, 1 in another (Chapter 15). Make a two-line toy file in the BED format and strip the chr:


Terminal (laptop)

printf 'chr1\t100\t200\nchr2\t300\t400\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.bed
sed 's/^chr//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.bed
cat ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/toy.bed

1   100 200
2   300 400
chr1    100 200
chr2    300 400
sed (stream editor) reads lines and writes them out, changed. s/^chr// is a substitution: s/pattern/replacement/, here “replace chr at the start of the line with nothing”. The file itself is unchanged, as cat shows: sed wrote the result to stdout, so save it with > to a new file. Each s changes the first match on a line; add g to change all of them:


Terminal (laptop)

echo 'a-b-c' | sed 's/-/_/'
echo 'a-b-c' | sed 's/-/_/g'

a_b-c
a_b_c
The pattern is a basic regular expression, as in grep. When the pattern contains /, pick another delimiter. File names from the URLs in the sample sheet:


Terminal (laptop)

tail -n +2 data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sed 's|.*/||'

SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357071_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357072_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357073_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357074_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357075_1.fastq.gz
SRR6357076_1.fastq.gz
s|.*/|| replaces “anything up to the last /” with nothing. (.* matches as much as it can.) sed can do much more, but substitution is what you need from it at this stage.
sed -i edits a file in place. It writes the changed text back into the file. Two rules: never on data/raw/, and always run the command without -i first and check the output. On a Mac, sed -i behaves differently in the system’s BSD sed (Chapter 7); this book uses GNU sed.






NoteOptional: FASTQ to FASTA with sed, and why to use seqkit instead





FASTA keeps only a header (starting with >) and the sequence. In a file with exactly four lines per read, GNU sed can convert:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 8 | sed -n '1~4s/^@/>/p;2~4p'

>SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932
CCTGAATCGAGAAGGAGGTGTCCAGGGAGTTCATCATCAGAATGATTAGTATGATTTACTGTAGATTCAGTAAGTTTCTGGCCTAAGATGAAGGTCGTGCT
>SRR6357070.6710070 6710070/1 kraken:taxid|4932
GTCAGATTGGAAGTCATGGTCAGATTCTATGTTAAGATCATCGGATTGTTGGATCTCATTTGACGCAATGAACGATTGATATGAAGCAGTTAAACGGTTTA
-n prints nothing unless told to; 1~4 means “line 1, then every 4th line” (GNU only), where @ becomes > and the line is printed; 2~4p prints the sequence lines. It works only because of the four-line layout. The format-aware command gives the same result with no such assumption:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit head -n 2 data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | pixi run seqkit fq2fa

Use seqkit fq2fa on real files.





6.8.2 awk: fields and computing
Start with a mistake. Print column 3 of the practice table:


Terminal (laptop)

awk '{print $3}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
awk -F'\t' '{print $3}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv

condition
3
control
control
treated
control
control
condition
treated
control
control
treated
control
control
The first version printed 3 for sample_C, instead of treated. By default awk splits each line into fields at any run of spaces or tabs, so the run folder Run 3 final became three fields. -F'\t' tells awk to split at tabs only. For tab-separated files, always use it.
awk reads its input one line (a record) at a time and splits it into fields, $1, $2, …; $0 is the whole line. A program is a list of pattern {action} pairs: for each line where the pattern is true, run the action. Either part may be missing: awk 'NR % 4 == 2' from Section 6.2 has a pattern and no action, which means “print the line”. Add up the reads column:


Terminal (laptop)

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 {s += $4} END {print s}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
tail -n +2 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv | sort -u | awk -F'\t' '{s += $4} END {print s}'

194
164
NR > 1 skips the header (NR is the record number); s += $4 adds field 4 to a running total s, which starts at 0; END { … } runs once, after the last line. 194 with the duplicated sample_B row, 164 without it, as promised in Section 6.5.
A filter with a condition, and output with tabs:


Terminal (laptop)

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 > 20' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 {print $1, $4}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/samples.tsv

sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_E    run5    treated 105
sample_B    run2    control 30
sample_C    12
sample_A    9
sample_B    30
sample_E    105
sample_B    30
sample_D    8
&& means “and”. In print $1, $4, the comma puts the output field separator between fields, a space by default; -v OFS='\t' makes it a tab, so the output is tab-separated too.
Fields in the annotation. A GTF line has nine tab-separated fields, and the ninth, the attributes, contains spaces (Figure 6.6). That is another reason for -F'\t'.




  A GTF line split by awk into nine tab-separated fields, $1 to $9. The line is the CDC19 transcript from the yeast test annotation. $1 seqname is I, $2 source is ensembl, $3 feature is transcript, $4 start is 71786, $5 end is 73288, $6 score is a dot, $7 strand is plus, $8 frame is a dot, and $9 attributes is gene_biotype "protein_coding"; gene_id "YAL038W"; gene_name "CDC19"; and more, shortened here. A tab separates each field from the next. Figure 6.6: A GTF line (the CDC19 transcript) split by awk -F'\t' into nine fields, $1 to $9, with the column names below. Field 9 contains spaces, so awk’s default splitting would break it apart.



Count transcripts per strand: column 3 is the feature and column 7 the strand.


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' | cut -f7 | sort | uniq -c

     60 -
     64 +
124 transcript lines: 64 on the plus strand and 60 on the minus strand. In this file each transcript has one line, and each gene one transcript, but that is a property of this file, not of GTF. == compares; text values go in double quotes.






NoteOptional: the longest transcript spans





For readers who want to see awk compute a column: the span of each transcript on the genome is end − start + 1. The match() part pulls the gene ID out of field 9; take it as given (GTF attributes are Chapter 17).


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz \
  | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript" {match($9, /gene_id "[^"]+"/); print $5 - $4 + 1, substr($9, RSTART + 9, RLENGTH - 10)}' \
  | sort -k1,1nr | head -n 3

4614 YAR050W
4416 YAL029C
4308 YAL024C
A span on the genome is not the length of the spliced transcript; coordinates are Chapter 17.



Check one tool against another. Add up the num_seqs column of the seqkit table you saved with tee:


Terminal (laptop)

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 {s += $4} END {print s}' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv

100000
100,000 reads in two files, and remembering Chapter 4’s meaning check: two mate files, so 50,000 read pairs. Now count the N bases (unknown bases) in each file with awk:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {n += gsub(/N/, "")} END {print n}'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {n += gsub(/N/, "")} END {print n}'

280
18842
gsub(/N/, "") removes every N from the line and returns how many it removed, and n adds them up. 280 and 18,842: exactly seqkit’s sum_n column from Chapter 4’s Exercise 2. (Every N also has the quality character #, the lowest score in this file, and no other base does: one more independent count that agrees.) Two independent tools agree, so you can trust the one-liner.






TipCheck a one-liner against something independent



Before trusting a new one-liner, compare it with a count you got another way: here awk’s N count and seqkit’s sum_n.





Table 6.7: The parts of awk used in this chapter.










Piece
Meaning
Example

{print $3}


$0

{print length($0)}

{print NF}

NR > 1, NR % 4 == 2


-F'\t'

awk -F'\t' …

replace all matches; returns the count

When a one-liner grows past one line, it belongs in a script (Chapter 8), or in R or Python (Chapter 12, Chapter 13), where it can be read, tested, and reused.

Check yourself. What does gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$7 == "-"' | wc -l count?






TipAnswer





Lines on the minus strand, of every feature type (transcripts, exons, CDS, codons): 296 here. Not genes.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.9 Compressed files
You have read .gz files through gunzip -c all chapter. gzip writes them too, and as a filter it compresses whatever arrives on stdin. Save the first 100 reads of R1 as a small compressed file, then check it:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | head -n 400 | gzip > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/small_R1.fastq.gz
gunzip -c ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/small_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l
gzip -t ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/small_R1.fastq.gz

400
400 lines, and gzip -t is silent: intact. 400 lines are 100 reads only in a file with four lines per read; the general recipe is pixi run seqkit head -n 100, as in Chapter 4.
Compress a stream you made yourself, the 50,000 sequence lines:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2' | gzip -c > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/seqs.txt.gz
ls -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/seqs.txt.gz

-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 853893 Nov 17 20:49 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/seqs.txt.gz
About 850 KB for 5.1 MB of text (the exact size depends on the gzip version). DNA compresses well because it uses only a few letters.
The family. gzip file compresses file into file.gz and removes the original; gunzip file.gz does the reverse. -c writes to stdout instead and leaves the input alone, which is what you want almost always. zcat file.gz is the same as gunzip -c file.gz in GNU gzip, and you will see it in other people’s scripts. This book writes gunzip -c because the zcat built into macOS does not read .gz files:
zcat: can't stat: data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz (data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz.Z): No such file or directory
(It looks for a .Z file, an older format.) On Linux, zcat works the same as gunzip -c.
Rules for big files.

Do not decompress a large file to disk to read it: stream it with gunzip -c … |. A 10 GB .fastq.gz is 40 GB or more uncompressed.
Many tools read .gz directly, including seqkit and most aligners, so a decompressed copy is rarely needed.
Reading a 10 GB file through a pipe is real work: on a cluster, do it in a job, not on the login node (Chapter 10).
bgzip is a variant of gzip that allows jumping to a position inside the file; indexed genomics files use it (Chapter 17). pigz is a parallel gzip that uses several cores (Chapter 35).




Table 6.8: Working with gzip files.










Task
Command
Note




check a file is intact
gzip -t f.gz
silent when intact (Chapter 1)


read
gunzip -c f.gz \| head
zcat on Linux; not macOS’s zcat


browse
zless f.gz
Chapter 5


search
zgrep -c pattern f.gz
same flags as grep


write compressed
cmd \| gzip > out.gz
never over the input


compress, keep original
gzip -k f
without -k, f is removed


indexable compression
bgzip f
for indexed genomics files (Chapter 17)


faster on many cores
pigz
Chapter 35












WarningPitfall: decompressing to disk



gunzip big.fastq.gz writes the full uncompressed file and deletes the .gz. Stream instead with gunzip -c big.fastq.gz | …, or give the .gz file to a tool that reads it directly.



Check yourself. Why stream a 10 GB .fastq.gz with gunzip -c … | instead of running gunzip file.fastq.gz first?






TipAnswer





No 40 GB or larger uncompressed copy on disk or in your quota, and the file is read once instead of twice.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.10 Text tools and format-aware tools
You did several jobs in this chapter with text tools. Each has a tool that understands the file format (Table 6.9).



Table 6.9: Text tools and format-aware tools for the jobs in this chapter.











Task
Text-tool way
Format-aware tool
Where the text tool breaks




count reads
wc -l ÷ 4, awk 'NR % 4 == 1'
seqkit stats
records not exactly four lines


count reads by header
grep -c '^@'
seqkit stats
quality lines that start with @


FASTQ to FASTA
sed -n '1~4s/^@/>/p;2~4p'
seqkit fq2fa
multi-line records


first N reads
head -n 400
seqkit head -n 100
multi-line records


reads with a motif
awk + grep -c
seqkit grep -s
both strands, mismatches
