awk -F'\t' '$3 == "exon"'
an annotation package (Chapter 17)
attribute parsing, comment lines


count alignments
(not text: BAM is binary)
samtools view -c (Chapter 16)
compressed binary format






The format-aware tool wins once files are real: records that span several lines (every NR % 4, head -n 400, and 1~4 in this chapter assumed four lines per read), comment and header lines, quoted fields, binary formats such as BAM, variants of compression, and the @ trap. Text tools stay the best way to look at a file and to check a result quickly: count lines, find the odd one, compare two columns. Part IV opens with the same principle.






ImportantKey idea



Use text tools to look and to check; use format-aware tools to process.

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.11 Summary

A pipe | joins one program’s stdout to the next one’s stdin, with no file in between. Build pipelines one step at a time and look at each step’s output.
> replaces a file and >> appends; the shell empties a > target before the command runs, so never redirect onto your input: write a new file, check it, mv it. tee saves and shows at once.
Results go to stdout and messages to stderr, by convention. 2>, 2>&1, and /dev/null route stderr on purpose; a pipeline’s status is its last command’s, so read the messages and check counts against what you expect.
cut, sort, uniq -c, and wc count and summarise columns; sort before uniq, use sort -n for numbers and LC_ALL=C for a reproducible order. grep finds lines and -c counts them.
A regular expression describes text (., [ ], *, +, ^, $, \); it is not a glob. sed 's/…/…/' substitutes; awk -F'\t' selects fields and computes. Stream .gz files with gunzip -c, and use format-aware tools to process real FASTQ, BAM, and annotation.




Table 6.10: The chapter’s commands on one page.









Task
Command




Pipe, save, append, show and save
cmd1 \| cmd2, > f, >> f, \| tee f


Errors to a file, both to a log, discard
2> err.txt, > log 2>&1, 2> /dev/null


Count lines, see invisible characters
wc -l, cat -A


Columns, count values
cut -f3, cut -d, -f1, sort \| uniq -c


Sort
sort -n, sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n, sort -k1,1nr, LC_ALL=C sort


Skip a header
tail -n +2


Find lines
grep -c, -v, -w, -o, -A 3, -E, -F


Substitute
sed 's/^chr//', sed 's|.*/||'


Fields and sums
awk -F'\t' '$3 == "x" {print $7}', awk 'NR > 1 {s += $4} END {print s}'


Compressed files
gunzip -c, \| gzip >, gzip -t, zgrep, zless


Compare two files
cmp a b (Exercise 3)

title: 6  Text tools and pipes
text:
6.12 Exercises
Run every exercise from ~/bioinf-computing, and write outputs to ~/bioinf-computing-ch06.

Exercise 1. Build a pipeline step by step. Start from gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | head -n 8 and add one step at a time, checking the output after each, until the pipeline reports how many reads of each length R2 has. Then remove the head. Record the final command and its result in NOTEBOOK.md.






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | head -n 8 | awk 'NR % 4 == 2'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | head -n 8 | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {print length($0)}'
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz | awk 'NR % 4 == 2 {print length($0)}' | sort | uniq -c

  50000 101
The same as R1: all 50,000 reads are 101 bases. Keeping head while you build makes each check instant.





Exercise 2. Fix the redirections. First make a copy of the seqkit table to work on:


Terminal (laptop)

cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv

Each of the four lines below has a redirection problem. Say what goes wrong, then write a fixed version. Run them only after you have predicted the result.


Terminal (laptop)

cut -f1,4 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/stats.tsv 2>&1
sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv

The third line empties the copy, so make it again before the fourth, and run the fourth line twice:


Terminal (laptop)

cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv >> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/files.txt

The goal: the per-file read counts saved in a file, seqkit’s table in stats.tsv and its messages in a log, the sorted table in its own file with the input untouched, and files.txt holding each file name once however often you run the line.






TipAnswer






The counts only go to the screen. Fix: add > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/reads_per_file.tsv.
2>&1 puts the [ERRO] lines, with their colour codes, into the results file, ahead of the header. Fix: > …/stats.tsv 2> …/stats.log.
The input is emptied before sort reads it (wc -c shows 0 bytes). Fix: > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_sorted.tsv, check it, and only then mv if you want to replace the original.
>> adds the names again on every run, so after two runs each name is there twice. Fix: >.

Start the fixed versions from a fresh copy, since line 3 emptied it:


Terminal (laptop)

cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts.tsv ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv
cut -f1,4 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/reads_per_file.tsv
pixi run seqkit stats -T ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/broken.fastq.gz > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/stats.tsv 2> ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/stats.log
sort -t$'\t' -k4,4n ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_sorted.tsv
cut -f1 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/counts_copy.tsv > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/files.txt

The fixed stats.tsv holds only the header, because the file is broken; the reason is in stats.log.





Exercise 3. Do the mates match? Aligners pair reads by position: read 1 in R1 with read 1 in R2, and so on (Chapter 15). Check that the two files list the same reads in the same order. In this file a header looks like @SRR6357070.25017281 25017281/1 kraken:taxid|4932 (R2: …/2 …): the mate number sits inside the second field, and the first field is the same in both mates. Write that field for every record, count the lines, and compare the files with cmp, which prints nothing when two files are identical:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz \
  | awk 'NR % 4 == 1 {print $1}' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt
gunzip -c data/raw/SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz \
  | awk 'NR % 4 == 1 {print $1}' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
wc -l ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
head -n 3 ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt
cmp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
echo $?

Then make a copy of ids_R2.txt with line 3 changed, and compare again:


Terminal (laptop)

sed '3s/$/x/' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2_bad.txt
cmp ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2_bad.txt
echo $?

Why are both the line count and cmp needed?






TipAnswer





  50000 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt
  50000 /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2.txt
 100000 total
@SRR6357070.25017281
@SRR6357070.6710070
@SRR6357070.5843839
0
/home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R1.txt /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch06/ids_R2_bad.txt differ: char 61, line 3
1
50,000 IDs in each file, identical and in the same order: cmp is silent and its status is 0. The altered copy differs at line 3 (sed '3s/$/x/' added an x to the end of line 3), status 1. cmp is also silent for two empty files, so the line count proves the extraction worked. This is a check for this four-line file; Chapter 15 does it with format-aware tools.





Exercise 4. Summarise the annotation. Using cut, sort, uniq -c, and awk -F'\t' on data/ref/genes.gtf.gz, and Figure 6.6 for the column numbers, find: the feature types and their counts; the sequence names and their counts; and the transcript lines per strand. Which line is on a sequence that is not in the genome? Note your commands and answers in NOTEBOOK.md.
Extension (optional). GTF attributes are Chapter 17, so these two commands are supplied. Run them and say what each counts:


Terminal (laptop)

gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | grep -o 'gene_id "[^"]*"' | sort -u | wc -l
gunzip -c data/ref/genes.gtf.gz | awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' \
  | grep -o 'gene_biotype "[^"]*"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr







TipAnswer





Feature types: the chapter’s pipeline, cut -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -k1,1nr: 129 exon, 124 transcript, 118 CDS, 115 start_codon, 114 stop_codon. Sequence names, cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c: 599 I, 1 not_in_genome. Strands, awk -F'\t' '$3 == "transcript"' | cut -f7 | sort | uniq -c: 60 -, 64 +. The odd line is line 1 (grep -n not_in_genome prints 1:), a CDS on not_in_genome.
Extension: 124 distinct gene IDs; and the gene types of the transcripts:
124
    116 gene_biotype "protein_coding"
      4 gene_biotype "tRNA"
      2 gene_biotype "pseudogene"
      1 gene_biotype "ncRNA"
      1 gene_biotype "snoRNA"





Exercise 5. Regex practice on the sample sheet. Write one grep -E that matches only the R2 file names in data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv, and count them. Then write one awk -F, command that prints the sample labels of the rows given as single-end, those with an empty fastq_2 (column 3).






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

grep -Eo 'SRR[0-9]+_2\.fastq\.gz' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv | wc -l
awk -F, '$3 == "" {print $1}' data/meta/samplesheet_upstream.csv

4
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP1
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2
Four R2 files, one per row with two files. RAP1_UNINDUCED_REP2 appears twice because the test sheet puts that label on two rows used as single-end; in the archive they are two different paired-end samples (Section 3.7). Without -o, grep -c would count lines, which is also 4 here.





Exercise 6. Check with a second tool. Count the R1 reads that contain the exact motif AGATCGGAAGAGC, first with grep -c on the sequence lines (as in Section 6.6), then with seqkit:


Terminal (laptop)

pixi run seqkit grep -s -P -C -p AGATCGGAAGAGC data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz

-s searches the sequences, -P the given (positive) strand only, -p gives the pattern, and -C counts the matching reads (seqkit’s -C, not grep’s -c). Do the numbers agree? Then make a one-read file that holds only the reverse complement of the motif, and run both tools on it, and seqkit once more without -P:


Terminal (laptop)

printf '@rc\nGCTCTTCCGATCT\n+\nIIIIIIIIIIIII\n' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq
awk 'NR % 4 == 2' ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq | grep -c AGATCGGAAGAGC
pixi run seqkit grep -s -P -C -p AGATCGGAAGAGC ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq
pixi run seqkit grep -s -C -p AGATCGGAAGAGC ~/bioinf-computing-ch06/revcomp.fastq







TipAnswer





On R1 both give 1,916. On the toy file, grep gives 0 and seqkit with -P gives 0, but seqkit without -P gives 1: by default seqkit grep -s searches both strands, and the reverse complement of the motif is the motif read from the other strand. On the real files both settings give 1,916 (R1) and 1,910 (R2), so only the toy file shows the difference. A second tool is a real check only when you know what each one counts.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.1 What this chapter does
Core. Work through it, with the exercises.
Part I asked you to run several “system” commands on trust. In Chapter 1 you pasted a block into ~/.bash_profile (Mac) that put the GNU tools first on your PATH. In 1 the pixi installer added a line to ~/.bashrc, bare seqkit said command not found while pixi run seqkit worked, and export EDITOR=nano lasted only until the terminal closed. In Chapter 3, chmod a-w made the raw reads read-only, yet rm -f could still delete a read-only file in a writable folder. This chapter explains each of these, so that when one goes wrong you know where to look.
The chapter has two halves, and it works well as two sittings. The first is about who may do what and how commands are found: permissions, making a script run, PATH, environment variables, and the startup files that set them. The second is about the running system: processes, disk space, the differences between Linux and macOS tools, and Windows line endings.
Commands run on your laptop. Everything that changes files happens in a scratch folder, ~/bioinf-computing-ch07; in the project, ~/bioinf-computing, you only look (ls -l, du). Two things you will deliberately change outside scratch: a few lines in your ~/.bashrc (Section 7.6, with a backup first) and your notes in NOTEBOOK.md. Make the scratch folder:
Two sections and the first exercise also read the practice folder ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/ from Chapter 5, without changing it. If you do not have it, paste the setup block from Section 5.2 first.
The Linux outputs shown were captured on Ubuntu 24.04 (bash 5.2.21, GNU coreutils 9.4, grep 3.11, sed 4.9, file 5.45), on a machine named laptop with the user you; macOS outputs on macOS 15 with the Mac’s own tools, where the text says so. Ubuntu 26.04, which WSL installs in late 2026, replaces most GNU core tools with a rewrite called uutils (Section 7.9); where its output differs, the text says so. Process numbers, dates, and sizes on your machine will differ.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.2 Who may do what: permissions
Every file and folder belongs to one user (its owner) and one group, and carries three sets of permissions. Start with who you are, then look at the raw reads you protected in Chapter 3:


Terminal (laptop)

whoami
id
cd ~/bioinf-computing
ls -ld data/raw
ls -l data/raw

you
uid=1000(you) gid=1000(you) groups=1000(you)
dr-xr-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Nov 17 11:22 data/raw
total 4372
-r--r--r-- 1 you you     112 Nov 17 11:22 checksums.md5
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2239317 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz
-r--r--r-- 1 you you 2232117 Nov 17 11:22 SRR6357070_2.fastq.gz
id gives your user, your main group, and every group you belong to (on your own laptop it may list more, such as sudo; on a cluster, your lab’s project groups). In ls -l, the two you columns are the owner and the group (Figure 5.4 in Chapter 5 named them). The first column is what this section explains.
Now name the parts (Figure 7.1). After the type letter (d folder, - file, l link) come three groups of three letters: for the user who owns it, for members of its group, and for other users. In each group, r is read, w is write, x is execute, and - means “not allowed”.




  Reading a permission string, part by part. Two examples: drwxr-x--- (a folder) and -rw-r--r-- (a file). The first character is the type: d for a folder, a dash for a file. The next nine characters are three triplets, for the user who owns the file, for its group, and for everyone else (other). In each triplet the places are r, w, and x, and a dash means that permission is off. Each letter is worth a number, r 4, w 2, x 1, and a dash 0; adding them gives one octal digit per triplet. drwxr-x--- gives 4+2+1 = 7, 4+0+1 = 5, and 0, so 750. -rw-r--r-- gives 4+2+0 = 6, 4, and 4, so 644. Below, what the letters mean. On a folder: r lists the names, x reaches the entries and lets you go inside, w adds, removes, and renames entries (and needs x too). On a file: r reads the contents, w changes the contents, x runs it.

Figure 7.1: Two permission strings taken apart: the type letter, then the user, group, and other triplets. Each triplet is also one digit, the sum of 4 (r), 2 (w), and 1 (x). On a folder the same letters mean something different (below).



On a file the letters mean what you would guess: read its contents, change its contents, run it as a program. On a folder they mean something else, and that is where most surprises come from. Try it in scratch, on a folder d holding one readable file, with the owner’s x removed:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm
mkdir d && echo hello > d/f
1chmod u-x d
ls -ld d
2\ls d
\ls -l d
cat d/f
cd d
3chmod u+x d


1

chmod changes permissions: u-x removes (-) execute (x) for the user (u). The full syntax follows below.

2

The backslash runs ls without any alias your system defines (Section 7.4); a colouring alias can change what ls tries to read.

3

Put x back, so the folder works again.


drw-r-xr-x 2 you you 4096 Nov 17 14:02 d
f
ls: cannot access 'd/f': Permission denied
total 0
-????????? ? ? ? ?            ? f
cat: d/f: Permission denied
bash: cd: d: Permission denied
(Ubuntu 26.04’s ls shows the ? line without the cannot access message.) ls d still lists the name f: reading a folder means reading its list of names, and you kept r. Everything about the entry fails: ls -l cannot read its details (the question marks), cat cannot open it although the file itself is readable, and cd cannot go in. On a folder, x (often called search permission) is what lets you reach the entries and pass through to anything below. The reverse also holds: with x but no r, ls d says cannot open directory 'd', yet cat d/f works if you know the name. Table 7.1 collects the cases.



Table 7.1: What each letter allows, on a file and on a folder, and the message you get without it.











Letter
On a file
On a folder
Without it




r
read the contents
list the names
cat: f: Permission denied; ls: cannot open directory 'd'


w
change the contents
add, remove, or rename entries (needs x too)
bash: f: Permission denied on >; rm: cannot remove 'd/f'


x
run it as a program
reach the entries, cd into it, pass through
bash: ./f: Permission denied; cd: d: Permission denied






Two rules make the letters predictable:

The classes are chosen, not added up. If you own the file, only the user triplet counts. An owner without x is refused even when “other” has x.
You need x on every folder on the way. cat ~/a/b/c/file.txt needs x on a, b, and c as well as r on the file.

Deleting is a change to the folder. Now Chapter 3’s surprise has its explanation. Removing a file takes its name out of the folder’s list, so rm needs w and x on the folder; the file’s own permissions do not matter. Creating a new file is also a change to the folder. Changing an existing file is not:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir locked && echo old > locked/data.txt
chmod a-w locked
echo new > locked/data.txt; cat locked/data.txt
echo x > locked/new.txt
rm locked/data.txt
chmod u+w locked

new
bash: locked/new.txt: Permission denied
rm: cannot remove 'locked/data.txt': Permission denied
The folder is read-only, yet data.txt was overwritten, because the file itself was still writable: only a new name or a removed name changes the folder. That is why Chapter 3 protected the files and the folder with chmod a-w data/raw/* data/raw. It also explains Chapter 6’s redirect into data/raw/: echo test > data/raw/notes.txt makes a new name, which the folder refuses; sort … > data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz targets an existing file, which the file’s missing w refuses.






ImportantKey idea



On a folder, r lists the names, x lets you reach the entries, and w (with x) lets you add, remove, or rename them. A file’s own permissions do not protect it from deletion; its folder’s do.


These are the ordinary permissions on your own disk. On a cluster, two more things can explain a refusal the letters do not: access control lists (ACLs), which grant extra users or groups access, and storage mounted so that nothing on it may run as a program, which turns ./script.sh into Permission denied whatever its letters say. If the string looks right and you are still refused, ask the help desk (Chapter 4).

7.2.1 Changing permissions with chmod
chmod takes a change and one or more names. The symbolic form says who, how, and what:

who: u (user), g (group), o (other), a (all three);
how: + add, - remove, = set exactly;
what: r, w, x.

You have used it twice already: chmod a-w (remove write for all, Chapter 3) and chmod 700 ~/.ssh (1). The second is the octal form: one digit per class, each the sum of r = 4, w = 2, x = 1 (Figure 7.1). So 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 5 = r-x, 4 = r--, 0 = ---, and 700 means the owner may do everything and nobody else anything. GNU stat prints both forms:


Terminal (laptop)

touch notes.txt && mkdir private
1stat -c '%A %a %n' notes.txt private
chmod u+x notes.txt && ls -l notes.txt
chmod 644 notes.txt && ls -l notes.txt
chmod go-rx private && stat -c '%A %a %n' private
umask


1

-c gives a format: %A the string, %a the octal number, %n the name. (macOS’s own stat has different options: Section 7.9.)


-rw-r--r-- 644 notes.txt
drwxr-xr-x 755 private
-rwxr--r-- 1 you you 0 Nov 17 14:04 notes.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you 0 Nov 17 14:04 notes.txt
drwx------ 700 private
0022
A symbolic change modifies the current permissions (u+x added one letter to whatever was there); an octal number sets all nine at once. So the same chmod a-w gave 555 on Chapter 3’s folder and 444 on its files only because they started at 755 and 644. Why do new files start at 644 and folders at 755? Your umask, 0022, removes w for group and other from every new file and folder. Sites can set a different umask: Nova’s is 0002, which leaves w for the group, so new files start at 664 and folders at 775, and your lab can edit them. SCINet’s Ceres and Atlas set 0027, so new files start at 640 and folders at 750: your group can read them but not change them, and other users cannot see them. On a cluster that does this, a labmate who must edit your file in a shared project folder needs you to run chmod g+w on it (Table 7.2). Check yours with umask; you rarely need to change it.



Table 7.2: Common permission changes. The “before” column matters for symbolic changes, which modify the current mode.











Goal
Before
Command
After




Protect raw data
-rw-r--r-- (644), folder drwxr-xr-x (755)
chmod a-w files folder
-r--r--r-- (444), dr-xr-xr-x (555)


Make a script runnable by you
-rw-r--r-- (644)
chmod u+x script.sh
-rwxr--r-- (744)


Private folder (~/.ssh)
any
chmod 700 folder
drwx------


Private key file
any
chmod 600 file
-rw-------


Let your group read a tree
-rw-------, drwx------
chmod -R g+rX folder
-rw-r-----, drwxr-x---


Undo a change
(note it first)
stat -c '%a' name, then chmod <that number> name
as before






There is no general “undo” for chmod: note the old mode first if you might want it back. Two more details for whole trees:

-R applies a change to a folder and everything inside it. chmod -R a+x folder makes every data file “executable” too (try it on a scratch folder and ls -l shows -rwxr-xr-x on plain files).
A capital X adds x only to folders and to files that are already executable for someone, and leaves ordinary data files alone. That is why g+rX in the table is safe on a tree of data.







WarningPitfall: chmod -R 777 is not a fix



777 lets every user on the machine change or delete your files. When you get Permission denied, read the permission string, find which letter is missing for whom, and add only that.








CautionMisconception: “When I get Permission denied, chmod 777 or sudo fixes it”



Reality. It hides which permission was missing and removes the protection for everyone. On a cluster you cannot use sudo at all. Read the string, then change one letter.




7.2.2 Try it: three ways to write the same permissions
Figure 7.2 shows the string, the octal number, and the symbolic chmod for any combination. Tick boxes and watch all three change; switch between file and folder to see what the letters mean. Try making 750, then 644, then the folder setting 700.

viewof permKind = Inputs.radio(["file", "folder"], {label: "Permissions on a", value: "file"})







viewof permUser = Inputs.checkbox(["r", "w", "x"], {label: "user (owner)", value: ["r", "w"]})







viewof permGroup = Inputs.checkbox(["r", "w", "x"], {label: "group", value: ["r"]})







viewof permOther = Inputs.checkbox(["r", "w", "x"], {label: "other", value: ["r"]})










{
  const classes = [
    {name: "user", key: "u", bits: permUser},
    {name: "group", key: "g", bits: permGroup},
    {name: "other", key: "o", bits: permOther}
  ];
  const letters = ["r", "w", "x"];
  const value = {r: 4, w: 2, x: 1};
  const isDir = permKind === "folder";
  const str = (isDir ? "d" : "-") + classes.map((c) =>
    letters.map((l) => c.bits.includes(l) ? l : "-").join("")).join("");
  const octal = classes.map((c) =>
    c.bits.reduce((s, l) => s + value[l], 0)).join("");
  const sym = classes.map((c) =>
    c.key + "=" + letters.filter((l) => c.bits.includes(l)).join("")).join(",");
  const name = isDir ? "folder" : "file.txt";
  const fileWords = {r: "read it", w: "change it", x: "run it"};
  const dirWords = {r: "list names", w: "add/remove entries", x: "reach entries"};
  const say = (c) => {
    const w = isDir ? dirWords : fileWords;
    const can = letters.filter((l) => c.bits.includes(l)).map((l) => w[l]);
    if (isDir && c.bits.includes("w") && !c.bits.includes("x"))
      return can.join(", ") + " (but w is useless without x)";
    return can.length ? can.join(", ") : "nothing";
  };
  const box = 40, gap = 6, groupGap = 30, left = 60, top = 40;
  const gx = (i) => left + i * (3 * box + 2 * gap + groupGap);
  return htl.svg`<svg class="diagram" viewBox="0 0 720 300" role="img"
      aria-label="${`${str}, octal ${octal}, chmod ${sym}`}">
    <text x="${left - 40}" y="${top + 27}" font-size="22" class="mono fill-muted">${isDir ? "d" : "-"}</text>
    ${classes.map((c, i) => htl.svg`<g>
      <text x="${gx(i) + (3 * box + 2 * gap) / 2}" y="${top - 12}" font-size="13"
            text-anchor="middle" class="fill-muted">${c.name}</text>
      ${letters.map((l, j) => {
        const on = c.bits.includes(l);
        return htl.svg`<g>
          <rect x="${gx(i) + j * (box + gap)}" y="${top}" width="${box}" height="${box}" rx="5"
                class="${on ? "fill-given-soft stroke-given" : "fill-surface stroke-line"}"/>
          <text x="${gx(i) + j * (box + gap) + box / 2}" y="${top + 27}" font-size="20"
                text-anchor="middle" class="mono ${on ? "fill-given" : "fill-muted"}">${on ? l : "-"}</text>
        </g>`;})}
      <text x="${gx(i) + (3 * box + 2 * gap) / 2}" y="${top + box + 26}" font-size="18"
            text-anchor="middle" class="mono">${c.bits.reduce((s, l) => s + value[l], 0)}</text>
    </g>`)}
    <text x="20" y="${top + 120}" font-size="15">String: <tspan class="mono" font-weight="700">${str}</tspan></text>
    <text x="20" y="${top + 146}" font-size="15">Octal: <tspan class="mono" font-weight="700">chmod ${octal} ${name}</tspan></text>
    <text x="20" y="${top + 172}" font-size="15">Symbolic: <tspan class="mono" font-weight="700">chmod ${sym} ${name}</tspan></text>
    ${classes.map((c, i) => htl.svg`<text x="20" y="${top + 204 + i * 20}" font-size="13.5" class="fill-muted">${c.name}: ${say(c)}</text>`)}
  </svg>`;
}








Figure 7.2: A permission calculator. The nine boxes are the letters of the string; each class’s digit is the sum of 4 (r), 2 (w), and 1 (x). The two chmod lines set exactly these permissions, in octal and in symbolic form.



If the figure does not load, the lesson is in Figure 7.1: rwxr-x---, 750, and u=rwx,g=rx,o= say the same thing.


7.2.3 Groups and shared folders
On a cluster, a lab shares files through a Unix group: a project folder such as /project/<name> on SCINet or /work/<group> on Nova belongs to the lab’s group, and members get the group’s permissions (Appendix A has each site’s details). When a labmate cannot read your file, check two things: which group owns it (ls -l) and whether that group may read it (the middle triplet). id shows which groups you are in; chgrp <group> file changes a file’s group to one of yours.
Two special settings appear on shared folders. You will mostly meet them, not set them; the site usually does:



Table 7.3: Two special permissions on shared folders (overview).










Setting
Shown as
On a folder




set-group-ID (setgid), chmod g+s
s in the group’s x place: drwxrws---
new files and folders inside get the folder’s group instead of your main group


sticky, chmod +t
t in other’s x place: drwxrwxrwt (as on /tmp)
in a folder everyone may write, only an entry’s owner may delete or rename it






Setgid decides the group of a new file, not whether the group may read it: the new file’s permissions still come from your umask (and any default ACLs). If files you create in a project folder come out unreadable to your lab, check their group and permissions with ls -l and ask the help desk what the site expects.
Here is what this looks like on Nova, in a group folder and a lab folder inside it (names replaced by <group>, <lab>, and you):
ls -ld /work/<group> /work/<group>/<lab>
cd /work/<group>/<lab>
touch group_test && ls -l group_test
umask
drwxrws--T. 43 root its-hpc-nova-<group> 44 Nov 18 12:11 /work/<group>
drwxrwsr-x. 16 you  its-hpc-nova-<group> 16 Nov 16 18:24 /work/<group>/<lab>
-rw-rw-r--. 1 you its-hpc-nova-<group> 0 Nov 20 12:34 group_test
0002
Both folders have the setgid s, so the new file belongs to the lab’s group, not to your main group (domain users on Nova). It is rw-rw-r-- because Nova’s umask is 0002, so your labmates can edit it. The group folder also has a capital T. That is the sticky bit on a folder that others can’t enter (no x for other); a lowercase t means the sticky bit plus x. The . after each permission string means the file has an SELinux security label, which you can ignore. Delete the test file with rm group_test when you are done.
SCINet’s Ceres follows the same pattern in /project/<name>, owned by root and the group proj-<name>, with two differences. Your main group there is a personal group named after you, so without the setgid s your files would belong to a group nobody else is in. And the umask is 0027, so the same touch gives -rw-r-----, and a folder you make gives drwxr-s---: your lab can read and enter, but not edit or add files, until you run chmod g+w on them. Atlas, SCINet’s other cluster, gives the same results; its project folder is drwxrws---, without the sticky T and without the SELinux ..
The GNU coreutils manual describes all of this in full.
Administrators and sudo. On your laptop, sudo runs one command as the administrator (root), for changes to the system itself, such as installing packages with apt. Never use it to fix permissions on your own files: files created by root in your home folder are a new problem. On a cluster you are not an administrator and this book never needs sudo: the book environment and later ones install into your own folders (1, Chapter 23).

Check yourself. (a) A folder is drwxr-xr-x and owned by you; a file in it is -r--r--r--. Can you delete the file? (b) What does chmod 640 notes.txt give, as a string? (c) A folder you own is drw-r--r--. Can you cat a readable file inside it?






TipAnswer






Yes. Deleting changes the folder, where you have w and x; the file’s own permissions do not matter. rm asks first because the file is read-only; rm -f does not ask. (b) -rw-r-----: you read and write, the group reads, others get nothing. (c) No. Without x on the folder you can list the names but not reach the entries.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.3 Making a script run
Chapter 3 ran its script as pixi run bash src/01_count_reads.sh: bash read the file. Scripts can also run as commands of their own. Make a one-line script in scratch (with nano or VS Code, or paste this) and try four ways to run it:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
1printf 'echo "hello from $0"\n' > hello.sh
bash hello.sh
./hello.sh
chmod u+x hello.sh
./hello.sh
hello.sh


1

$0 is the name the script was started as (Chapter 8).


hello from hello.sh
bash: ./hello.sh: Permission denied
hello from ./hello.sh
bash: hello.sh: command not found



Table 7.4: Four ways to run the same file.











Command
Result
Exit status
Why




bash hello.sh
runs
0
bash reads the file; it need not be executable


./hello.sh
Permission denied
126
found, but not allowed to run: no x


chmod u+x hello.sh, then ./hello.sh
runs
0
now executable


hello.sh
command not found
127
without a /, bash searches PATH, and this folder is not on it (Section 7.4)






The exit statuses join Chapter 4’s echo $?: 126 means “found but cannot run”, 127 “not found”. ./hello.sh works because . is the current folder, so ./hello.sh is a path, and a name with a / in it is run directly, with no search.
The shebang line. Add one line at the very top of the file:


hello.sh

#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "hello from $0"

When a file with the x bit is run, the kernel reads its first line. If it starts with #! (said “shebang”), the rest names the program that should read the file, and the kernel starts that program with the file’s name (Figure 7.3). Without a shebang, bash happens to run the file as a bash script, but other programs that start it may not; always write one. It must be the very first line, starting at the first character.




  What happens when you type ./hello.sh, in five steps. 1: the shell sees a slash in the name, so it treats ./hello.sh as a path and runs that file, with no search of PATH. 2: the kernel checks the file's x (execute) bit; without it the run stops with bash: ./hello.sh: Permission denied (exit status 126), and with it the run goes on. 3: the kernel reads line 1, the shebang #!/usr/bin/env bash, which names the program that runs the file. 4: env finds bash on PATH, bash runs the file, and the terminal shows hello from ./hello.sh. 5: the same file saved with Windows (CRLF) line endings: line 1 really ends in an invisible \r, so env looks for a program called bash\r, finds none, and prints /usr/bin/env: 'bash\r': No such file or directory (exit status 127).
  You type ./hello.sh. The name holds a slash, so the shell treats it as a path to a file and does not search PATH.
  The kernel checks the file's x bit. Without it, the run stops with Permission denied (exit status 126); with it, the run goes on.
  The kernel reads line 1. A shebang, #! and a path, names the program that should run the file: here /usr/bin/env, asked for bash.
  env searches PATH for bash and starts it on the file. bash runs the commands, and the script prints its greeting.
  The same script saved with Windows line endings: line 1 ends in an invisible \r, so env looks for a program named bash\r, finds none, and the run fails with exit status 127.
  
  
  YOU TYPE
  ./hello.sh
  a script in the folder you are in

    so it runs that file; no PATH search
    ./hello.sh

    -rwxr-xr-x  hello.sh
    
    ✓ x set: go on
    
    ✗ no x: exit 126

    The kernel reads line 1, the shebang
    
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
  
  #! names the program that runs the file

    \r
  
  
  
    
    
    4
  
  
    env finds bash on PATH; bash runs the file
    the rest of the file is bash commands
    
    ✓ found: /usr/bin/bash
  
  
    env looks for a program named bash\r
    no program has that name, so nothing runs
    
    ✗ no program called bash\r
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  TERMINAL

    the shell decides: a path, not a command name
  
  
    bash: ./hello.sh: Permission denied
    if the x bit is missing · exit 126
    chmod +x hello.sh adds it
  
  
    (nothing printed yet: the kernel is choosing the program)
  
  
    hello from ./hello.sh
    exit 0
  
  
    /usr/bin/env: 'bash\r': No such file or directory
    exit 127
  




Figure 7.3: What happens when you type ./hello.sh. A path skips the PATH search; the kernel checks the x bit, reads the shebang line, and env finds bash. The last step shows a file saved with Windows line endings, whose shebang names a program that does not exist (Section 7.10). Use Next to step through.



This book’s scripts use #!/usr/bin/env bash, as Chapter 3’s script already does. env looks bash up on your PATH, so on a Mac it finds the current bash from Chapter 1 instead of Apple’s /bin/bash, which is version 3.2 from 2007 (/bin/bash --version on a Mac prints GNU bash, version 3.2.57). Inside pixi run or pixi shell it finds the environment’s programs the same way. R and Python scripts follow the same pattern, #!/usr/bin/env Rscript and #!/usr/bin/env python3 (Chapter 12, Chapter 13).






CautionMisconception: “To run a script I must type bash script.sh”



Reality. With a shebang line and the x bit, a script runs as ./script.sh, and by name alone once its folder is on PATH. bash script.sh ignores the shebang: bash plot.py tries to read Python as shell commands and fails.








ImportantKey idea



A command runs as a program when the shell can find it (a path, or a folder on PATH), the file has the x bit, and its first line names an interpreter that exists.



Check yourself. ./run.sh says Permission denied, but bash run.sh works. What is missing, and what is the fix?






TipAnswer





The x bit. bash run.sh only needs to read the file; ./run.sh needs permission to run it. chmod u+x run.sh.

title: 7  The Linux system
section: 7.4 How the shell finds a command: PATH
text:
7.4 How the shell finds a command: PATH
When you type a name without a /, such as ls or seqkit, bash looks for a program file with that name in a list of folders. The list is the variable PATH:


Terminal (laptop)

1echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n'


1

PATH is one line with folders separated by :; tr turns each : into a newline (Chapter 6).


/home/you/.pixi/bin
/usr/local/sbin
/usr/local/bin
/usr/sbin
/usr/bin
/sbin
/bin
Bash searches these folders in order, top to bottom, and runs the first match. ~/.pixi/bin is first because 1’s pixi installer added it to the front. Your list will be longer or ordered differently: Ubuntu adds /usr/games and /snap/bin, and on a Mac after Chapter 1 the GNU folders come first.
Which copy runs? type -a asks bash for every match, in the order bash would use them:


Terminal (laptop)

type -a ls
type cd

ls is aliased to `ls --color=auto'
ls is /usr/bin/ls
ls is /bin/ls
cd is a shell builtin
Three kinds of answer appear here. An alias is a shortcut bash expands before anything else: on Ubuntu, and on Nova, typing ls really runs ls --color=auto, which colours the names. Then come the program files on PATH: two here, because current Ubuntu keeps /bin as another name for /usr/bin, so both entries reach the same file. And cd is a builtin, part of bash, with no file at all (Chapter 5). On a Mac after Chapter 1 the answer differs:
ls is /usr/local/opt/coreutils/libexec/gnubin/ls
ls is /bin/ls
The GNU ls comes first, then Apple’s own (/opt/homebrew/… on Apple silicon). That order is what Chapter 1’s gnubin lines arranged.
So the full order is: aliases, then functions (named groups of commands, Chapter 8), then builtins, then the folders of PATH. Changing PATH cannot override an alias or builtin of the same name. alias alone lists your aliases; a backslash (\ls) or command ls runs the program without the alias, as you did in Section 7.2.
The book’s environment. Now the explanation 1 promised. From the project folder:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing
type -a seqkit
pixi run bash -c 'type -a seqkit; echo "$PATH" | tr ":" "\n" | head -n 3'

bash: type: seqkit: not found
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin/seqkit
/home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin
/home/you/.pixi/bin
/usr/local/sbin
No folder on your PATH holds seqkit, hence Chapter 4’s command not found. pixi run starts one command with the environment’s bin folder put first on PATH, so the environment’s copy is found and wins over any other. pixi shell does the same for a whole new shell, until you type exit (Figure 7.4).




  How the shell finds a command on PATH, in four steps. PATH is a list of folders, searched from the top down: /home/you/.pixi/bin, /usr/local/bin, /usr/bin, /bin. 1: in a plain terminal no folder holds seqkit, and the shell prints bash: seqkit: command not found (exit status 127). 2: pixi run puts the project environment's folder, /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin, on top, and seqkit is found there. 3: an old copy of seqkit in /home/you/bin sits above it on PATH; the first match wins, so the old copy runs and the environment's copy is never reached. 4: type -a seqkit lists every match in PATH order: seqkit is /home/you/bin/seqkit, then seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin/seqkit.
  In a plain terminal the shell looks for seqkit in each PATH folder, top to bottom. None holds it, so you get command not found (exit status 127).
  pixi run puts the project environment's bin folder at the top of PATH, so the shell finds seqkit there first.
  An old copy in /home/you/bin sits higher on PATH. The search stops at the first match, so the old copy runs and the environment's copy is never reached.
  type -a seqkit lists every match in PATH order, so you can see which copy runs (the first line) and which ones are hidden behind it.
  
    
      
    
  
  
  The shell looks for seqkit in each PATH folder, top to bottom
  the first folder that holds it wins; the search stops there

  last

    your own folder

    never reached
  
  
  
    
    
    
    
  
  
    /home/you/.pixi/bin
    /usr/local/bin

    /bin
  
  
    ✗ no seqkit
    ✗ no seqkit
    ✗ no seqkit
    ✗ no seqkit
  
  
    not searched
    not searched
    not searched
    not searched
  
  
  
  TERMINAL
  
    seqkit
    bash: seqkit: command not found
    a plain terminal, outside the project
    exit 127
  
  
    pixi run seqkit
    runs /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin/seqkit
  
  
    seqkit
    runs /home/you/bin/seqkit: the old copy, not the project's
  
  
    type -a seqkit

    1st: this one runs
    2nd: hidden
  




Figure 7.4: How bash finds seqkit: it checks each PATH folder from the top and runs the first match. In a plain terminal nothing matches; pixi run puts the environment’s folder on top; a second copy higher up would win instead; type -a lists every match in order. Use Next to step through.



The wrong copy. If two copies are on PATH, the first wins, even if it is older. This is what Chapter 4 warned about: a bare seqkit might run some other installation, with a different version. Check with type -a seqkit and seqkit version; inside the book, pixi run makes the environment’s copy win. On a cluster, module load also works by changing PATH (Chapter 10), so a module loaded beside pixi shell can put a second copy in front. Exercise 3 sets up a fake seqkit to show this safely.
which seqkit is a common alternative, but it is a separate program, its versions behave differently, and its answer need not match what bash will run. Usually it knows nothing of your aliases; on Nova which ls shows the alias too, because there type which reports which is a function: the site wraps the real /usr/bin/which in a shell function that passes it your aliases and functions. Use bash’s own type -a. Table 7.5 collects the commands.



Table 7.5: Commands for finding out what runs.










Command
Tells you
Use it when




type -a name
every alias, builtin, and file bash would use, in order
first choice, in bash


type name
the one bash will use
a quick check


command -v name
what will run, in one line
in scripts (Chapter 8)


which name
a file on PATH, by a separate program
other people’s notes; prefer type -a


echo "$PATH" \| tr ':' '\n'
the folders searched, in order
command not found


hash -r
(forgets remembered locations)
after moving or installing a program in the same terminal






The last row: bash remembers where it found each command, so after you move or install a program, hash -r (or a new terminal) makes it look again.
Changing PATH. Put a folder of your own in front of the existing list:


Terminal (laptop)

export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"

$PATH on the right is the old list, so this adds one folder and keeps the rest. It is the same shape as the gnubin line in Chapter 1’s ~/.bash_profile and the line the pixi installer added to ~/.bashrc. It lasts for this terminal only; Section 7.6 makes such lines permanent. Two mistakes to avoid:

Replacing instead of adding. PATH=~/bin leaves only one folder, and every ordinary command fails with command not found. Open a new terminal to recover, or run export PATH=/usr/bin:/bin to get the basics back.
Putting . (the current folder) on PATH. Then whatever folder you are in can supply a program called ls. Type ./script.sh instead.







ImportantKey idea



For a name without a /, bash checks aliases, functions, and builtins, then searches the PATH folders top to bottom and runs the first match. type -a shows every match in that order.








CautionMisconception: “Once I install a tool, it works in every terminal”



Reality. (From 1, now with the mechanism.) A tool runs by name only if its folder is on that shell’s PATH. The book environment’s folder is added by pixi run and pixi shell, for that command or shell only; a module’s by module load.



Check yourself. type -a samtools prints samtools is /home/you/bin/samtools, then samtools is /usr/bin/samtools. Which runs when you type samtools, and how would you run the other one?






TipAnswer





The first, ~/bin/samtools, because ~/bin comes earlier on PATH. Run the other by its path, /usr/bin/samtools.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.5 Environment variables
PATH is one of many variables the shell keeps. Look at a few:


Terminal (laptop)

echo "$HOME"
echo "$USER"
echo "$SHELL"

/home/you
you
/bin/bash
env | sort | less lists the dozens of variables that every program started from this shell receives, one NAME=value per line (q quits). Now see the difference between a variable that stays in the shell and one that is passed on. bash -c '…' starts a second bash, a child of this one, that runs one line and exits:


Terminal (laptop)

x=1
bash -c 'echo "child sees x=[$x]"'
export x
bash -c 'echo "child sees x=[$x]"'

child sees x=[]
child sees x=[1]
Now name it. x=1 makes a shell variable, which lives only in this shell. export turns it into an environment variable, which is copied into every program this shell starts: scripts, R, Python, seqkit. Copies only go down, from parent to child. A script cannot change the variables of the shell that started it, which is why pixi shell has to start a new shell rather than change yours. A second terminal opened separately is not a child of the first, so it never sees an export you typed in the first. Once a variable is exported it stays exported: a later x=2 changes the value children see, without a second export. That is why PATH, already exported when your shell starts, can be changed with a plain assignment.
Two details. No spaces around =: x = 1 runs a command called x (bash: x: command not found); quoting and the rest are Chapter 8. And SHELL names your configured login shell, not necessarily the shell you are typing in; to check you are in bash, use Chapter 1’s echo "$BASH_VERSION".
A variable can last for one command, one terminal, or every new terminal (Table 7.6).

Write the variable in front of the command, with no export: TMPDIR=~/bigtmp sort big.txt gives sort a different folder for its temporary files, for that run only.

Your locale settings. Chapter 6 used LC_ALL=C sort to get the same sort order everywhere. The locale is the group of LANG and LC_* variables that sets language, sort order, and number format; locale prints yours:


Terminal (laptop)

locale | head -n 6

LANG=en_US.UTF-8
LANGUAGE=
LC_CTYPE="en_US.UTF-8"
LC_NUMERIC="en_US.UTF-8"
LC_TIME="en_US.UTF-8"
LC_COLLATE="en_US.UTF-8"
LC_COLLATE is the one that decides sort order; LC_ALL, if set, overrides all the others. This book leaves your default alone and sets LC_ALL=C in front of a single command when the order must be reproducible. A cluster may use a different default (often C or en_US.UTF-8), so check locale there too. Text encodings themselves are Chapter 36.

Check yourself. You run export THREADS=4 in one terminal, then open a second terminal and run echo "$THREADS". What prints, and what would make the setting reach every new terminal?






TipAnswer





An empty line. export reaches the shell it was typed in and the programs that shell starts; a separately opened terminal is not one of them. A line export THREADS=4 in ~/.bashrc reaches every new terminal.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.6 Startup files: .bashrc and .bash_profile
Every time bash starts, it may first read a startup file of commands from your home folder. That is how the pixi installer’s PATH line reaches every new terminal. Which file it reads depends on two questions about how bash was started. Ask them in the terminal you have open, and in a second bash started inside it:


Terminal (laptop)

shopt -q login_shell && echo login || echo "not login"
[[ $- == *i* ]] && echo interactive || echo "not interactive"
bash -l -c 'shopt -q login_shell && echo login || echo "not login"'
bash -c '[[ $- == *i* ]] && echo interactive || echo "not interactive"'

not login
interactive
login
not interactive
(Copy these as they are; && and || are Chapter 8.) This output is from a terminal window on desktop Ubuntu, which is interactive (you type into it) but not a login shell; so is VS Code’s terminal on Linux and WSL, and a bash typed inside a shell. bash -l starts a login shell, and a bash -c that just runs a line is not interactive. An SSH login is both login and interactive; so is a new Ubuntu window on WSL (Windows Terminal, or wsl typed in PowerShell), a new Terminal window on a Mac, and VS Code’s terminal on a Mac with 1’s -l setting. There the first line says login, and bash’s own messages start with -bash: instead of bash:. Run the first two lines in each place you open a shell, including your cluster, to see what yours are.
Now name it (Table 7.8, Figure 7.5). These are the rules from the Bash manual for the cases you will meet:



Table 7.8: Which of your startup files bash reads.










How bash starts
Example
Reads




interactive login
SSH login; new WSL window; Mac Terminal; bash -l
the first one that exists of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile


interactive, not login
new desktop Ubuntu terminal; VS Code’s terminal on Linux/WSL; bash typed in a shell
~/.bashrc


not interactive (a script)
bash script.sh, ./script.sh, a job script
neither (unless the variable BASH_ENV names a file)


a command over SSH
ssh host command
often ~/.bashrc (bash’s special case for remote commands; Nova and Ceres do)










  Which startup files bash reads, by how it starts. An interactive login shell (an SSH login, a new WSL window, the macOS Terminal, or bash --login) reads the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, and ~/.profile that exists, and only that one. An interactive shell that is not a login shell (a new terminal on desktop Ubuntu, VS Code's terminal on Linux or WSL, or bash typed inside a shell) reads ~/.bashrc. ssh host command, which runs one command with no prompt, often reads ~/.bashrc too. A script, a non-interactive shell, reads no startup file (only the file named in BASH_ENV, if that is set). The book's setup has ~/.bash_profile read ~/.bashrc, as Ubuntu's ~/.profile already does, so every interactive shell ends up with the same settings.

    from ~/.bash_profile (Ubuntu: ~/.profile)

Figure 7.5: Which startup file bash reads, by how it was started. A login shell reads the first of three files that exists; an interactive non-login shell reads ~/.bashrc; a script reads neither. In the book’s setup the login file reads ~/.bashrc too, so settings in ~/.bashrc reach every interactive shell.



System-wide files such as /etc/profile are read as well; they are set by whoever runs the machine (Appendix A for the clusters).
The book’s setup. Login and non-login shells read different files, which would mean writing every setting twice. Instead, the login file reads ~/.bashrc:

on a Mac, the last lines of Chapter 1’s ~/.bash_profile block do it (if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi; . reads a file into the current shell);
on Ubuntu and WSL, the ~/.profile that comes with a new account does the same;
on a cluster, the site’s default files usually do; check (below).

So put your settings in ~/.bashrc, and every interactive shell gets them. Now reread Chapter 1’s block line by line: Homebrew’s shellenv sets PATH for Homebrew, the gnubin loop puts the GNU tools first and the export passes PATH and MANPATH on, and the last line reads ~/.bashrc.
One trap on Ubuntu, WSL, and clusters: bash reads only the first login file that exists. If you create a ~/.bash_profile (even an empty one), bash stops reading ~/.profile, and with it the line that reads ~/.bashrc. Check which files you have:


Terminal (laptop)

1ls -a ~ | grep -E '^\.(bash|profile)'
2grep -n bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.bash_login ~/.profile 2>/dev/null


1

grep -E with a regular expression (Chapter 6): names starting with .bash or .profile.

2

Which login file reads ~/.bashrc, and on which line; 2>/dev/null hides the messages for files you do not have.


A script that sees one of your variables usually inherited it from the shell that started it (it was exported there); that does not mean the script read ~/.bashrc.

7.6.1 Changing ~/.bashrc safely
Make 1’s EDITOR setting permanent. First a backup, with cp -n so that a second try never overwrites the first backup (Chapter 5; ignore the non-portable warning Ubuntu’s cp prints):


Terminal (laptop)

cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07
1echo 'export EDITOR=nano' >> ~/.bashrc
tail -n 2 ~/.bashrc


1

>> appends. A single > would replace your whole ~/.bashrc with this one line (Chapter 6).


Then open a new terminal and check with echo "$EDITOR". (To apply the file to the terminal you are in, source ~/.bashrc reads it again; a new terminal is the honest test.) Rules for every change:

Back up first, and keep one working terminal open while you test in a new one. If a broken file stops new terminals from working, bash --noprofile --norc starts a clean shell to fix it from, or restore the backup.
Nothing in ~/.bashrc should print text. A command run over SSH may read it (Table 7.8), and output there can break rsync and older scp (Chapter 9). Put anything that prints inside if [[ $- == *i* ]]; then … fi, which runs only in interactive shells.
On a cluster, keep the site’s lines, and do not load modules or start environments from startup files: they would change every terminal and every remote command without asking, and make a job’s software depend on your dotfiles (Chapter 10, Appendix A).







WarningPitfall: a .bashrc that prints text



Output from ~/.bashrc can break rsync and scp. Back up before editing, keep a working terminal open, and test in a new one.


Things worth putting there. A few settings earlier chapters pointed here:


~/.bashrc (additions)

export EDITOR=nano                 # @sec-book-setup
HISTSIZE=10000                     # remember more history (@sec-shell-basics)
HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth             # skip duplicates and lines starting with a space
alias ll='ls -l'                   # a shortcut of your own
PS1='\u@\h:\w\$ '                  # the prompt: user@host:folder$


History: HISTSIZE is how many commands a shell remembers (Ubuntu sets 1000); ignoreboth skips repeated lines and lines you start with a space. These are the settings Chapter 5 mentioned.
Aliases: alias ll='ls -l' makes ll mean ls -l (Ubuntu’s default ~/.bashrc already defines it as ls -alF). Aliases are used only in interactive shells, never in scripts, so do not rely on them in anything you share.
The prompt: the prompt is the variable PS1. \u is your user, \h the machine, \w the folder, so the line above gives you@laptop:~/bioinf-computing$, the prompt Chapter 5 described. Try a new PS1 in one terminal first; it disappears when you close it. Keep the host name in it on a cluster: it tells you whether you are on a login node or a compute node (Chapter 10).
noclobber: you could add set -o noclobber (Chapter 6), but this book does not, because later chapters overwrite files on purpose.


Check yourself. You added export EDITOR=nano to ~/.bashrc on the cluster, but a new SSH login does not see it. What do you check?






TipAnswer





An SSH login reads the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile that exists. Find which one that is (ls -a ~), and whether it reads ~/.bashrc (grep -n bashrc on it). If not, add if [ -f ~/.bashrc ]; then . ~/.bashrc; fi to that file.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.7 Processes
Start a command that takes a while, and stop it:


Terminal (laptop)

1sleep 300


1

sleep waits for the given number of seconds and does nothing else: a safe stand-in for a long analysis. Press Ctrl-CCtrl-C while it waits.


^C
Then check its exit status with echo $?: 130, the number a command gets when Ctrl-CCtrl-C stops it. Now run it in the background by ending the line with &, so the prompt comes back at once, and look at what is running:


Terminal (laptop)

sleep 300 &
jobs
ps
kill %1
jobs

[1] 3219
[1]+  Running                 sleep 300 &
    PID TTY          TIME CMD
   3217 pts/0    00:00:00 bash
   3219 pts/0    00:00:00 sleep
   3220 pts/0    00:00:00 ps
[1]+  Terminated              sleep 300
[1] 3219 is the job number (1, for this terminal) and the process ID (PID, 3219, for the whole machine). jobs lists this terminal’s jobs; ps lists the processes started from this terminal: your shell, the sleep, and ps itself. kill %1 ended job 1; kill 3219 would have done the same by PID. (On a Mac, bash prints Terminated: 15.)
Now name it. A process is a running program, with a PID, an owner, and a parent: the process that started it, here your shell. Every program you have run, from ls to seqkit, ran as a process and ended. Your shell is a process too, and runs builtins such as cd and export inside itself, without starting a new one (Chapter 5). Figure 7.6 shows the states a process can be in, and how you move it between them.




  The life of a process started from the shell, as a state diagram, using sleep 300. Typed as is, it runs in the foreground and holds the terminal; typed as sleep 300 &, it starts in the background and the prompt comes back. Ctrl-Z stops a foreground process: it is paused but still holds its memory. From stopped, fg brings it back to the foreground and bg lets it run in the background; fg also brings a background job to the foreground. A process ends with Ctrl-C (sends SIGINT, which asks it to stop; reaches only the foreground), kill (sends SIGTERM, which also asks), or kill -9 (sends SIGKILL, which forces it and cannot be caught). kill and kill -9 work on any job. The shell is the parent of every job it starts.
  
    
      
    
    
      
    
  
  
  you type
  
  sleep 300
  the shell (bash) is
  the parent of every job
  
  
  Foreground
  holds the terminal
  
  Background
  runs; prompt free
  
  Stopped
  paused
  still holds its memory
  
  Ended
  process exits
  
  
  as is
  
  sleep 300 &

  kill
