  asks
  
  kill -9 SIGKILL: forces
  
  kill and kill -9 work on any job; Ctrl-C reaches only the foreground.




Figure 7.6: The life of a process started from your shell. & and bg run it in the background, fg brings it back; Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z stops it, still holding its memory, until fg, bg, or kill. Ctrl-CCtrl-C and kill ask it to end; kill -9 forces it.



A program in the foreground has your keyboard; one in the background runs while you type other commands. To stop a program, the shell sends it a signal (Table 7.9).



Table 7.9: Ways to stop a process, and what the program can do about each.











Key or command
Signal
The program can
Use it




Ctrl-CCtrl-C
SIGINT (interrupt)
clean up first, or ignore it
to stop the foreground command


kill PID or kill %1
SIGTERM (terminate), the default
clean up first, or ignore it
to end a background or stuck process


kill -9 PID
SIGKILL
nothing: ended at once
last resort, when kill alone did not work


Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z
SIGTSTP (stop)
(it pauses)
rarely on purpose; see the pitfall






Ctrl-CCtrl-C and kill ask: a well-written tool deletes its half-written files and exits. kill -9 cannot be caught, so the program gets no chance to clean up: look for and delete partial output files afterwards. You can signal only your own processes.
Stopped is not ended. Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z pauses the foreground program and gives you the prompt back. It looks like a way out, but the program is still there:


Terminal (laptop)

sleep 600

Press Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z, then:


Terminal (laptop)

jobs
1ps -o pid,stat,rss,command
exit


1

-o chooses columns: stat the state (T stopped, S sleeping, R running), rss the memory it holds, in kB, command the command line. Linux also accepts cmd, but the Mac’s ps does not.


^Z
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 600
[1]+  Stopped                 sleep 600
    PID STAT   RSS COMMAND
   3217 S     4776 bash
   3221 T     1952 sleep 600
   3222 R+    4152 ps -o pid,stat,rss,command
exit
There are stopped jobs.
Bash refuses the first exit to warn you. (In a login shell, such as a WSL window or a Mac Terminal, exit prints logout first.) Resume the job with fg (foreground) or bg (background), or end it with kill %1. A large analysis stopped with Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z keeps all its memory until then.






WarningPitfall: Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z does not stop a program for good



It pauses it, still holding its memory. Use Ctrl-CCtrl-C to stop a command; if you pressed Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z, finish with fg or kill %1.


Some clusters switch Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z off (SCINet’s Ceres and Atlas leave it on). On Nova, a site startup file (/etc/profile.d/disable-control-z.sh) runs stty susp undef, so the key does nothing and the command keeps running: no paused jobs are left holding memory on a shared login node. stty -a shows susp = <undef> when the key is off, and susp = ^Z when it works. Press Ctrl-CCtrl-C instead, which still works there.
Watching the machine: top. top shows the busiest processes, updated every few seconds; q quits. Here two busy test processes run alongside everything else (Linux top, sorted by CPU):
top - 14:25:42 up  9:05,  1 user,  load average: 0.38, 0.28, 0.19
Tasks:   9 total,   3 running,   5 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
%Cpu(s):  6.7 us,  5.5 sy,  0.0 ni, 87.7 id,  0.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
MiB Mem :   7837.4 total,   3956.1 free,   1369.3 used,   2810.8 buff/cache
MiB Swap:   1024.0 total,   1024.0 free,      0.0 used.   6468.1 avail Mem

    PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU  %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
   3233 you       20   0    5688   1820   1820 R 100.0   0.0   0:02.21 yes
   3232 you       20   0    5688   1836   1836 R 100.0   0.0   0:02.20 yes
The columns to read first:

%CPU: in Linux top’s usual display, 100% is one logical CPU (Chapter 1’s cores and threads). A tool running on four threads can show about 400%.
RES: the memory it really holds, in kB unless marked (m, g).
USER and COMMAND: whose it is and what it is.

On Linux, press M to sort by memory and P by CPU. macOS top looks different and sorts with top -o cpu or top -o mem (Section 7.9). htop, where installed, is a friendlier version with the same information; this book uses top, which every system has.
On a cluster. Do not rely on a command started in an ordinary SSH terminal surviving when the connection drops, and do not rely on closing the window to stop everything you started either: what happens depends on how the program was started and how it handles signals (the Bash manual’s Signals has the rules). For work that must keep running, use the site’s persistent sessions (tmux, Chapter 9), or submit it to the scheduler as a job, whose life does not depend on your window at all (Chapter 10). On a login node, ps -u "$USER" or top -u "$USER" lists only your own processes, so you can find and end leftovers. You need the -u: on Nova, top’s header showed 41 users and 1,714 processes on one login node, and on Ceres 62 users and 1,165. (top cuts long user names to eight characters, so first.last shows as first.+; -u still takes the full name.) Heavy work belongs in a job, not on the login node (Chapter 1).






CautionMisconception: “Closing the window decides whether my command keeps running”



Reality. Neither “it keeps going” nor “it always stops” is safe to assume. Run long work in tmux (Chapter 9) or as a scheduler job (Chapter 10), and check with ps -u "$USER".



Check yourself. top shows your python at 400% CPU. How many CPUs is it using? And what is the difference between Ctrl-CCtrl-C and Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z?






TipAnswer





About four logical CPUs, in Linux top’s usual display (100% is one). Ctrl-CCtrl-C asks the program to end; Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z only pauses it, and it keeps its memory until fg, bg, or kill.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.8 Disk usage: df and du
Two questions come up all the time: how much space is left, and what is using it. Chapter 1 used df -h ~ for the first:


Terminal (laptop)

df -h ~

Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sdd       1007G  2.0G  954G   1% /
df reports a whole filesystem: one disk or storage area, named in the first column and reached through the folder in the last. (Your first column will differ: /dev/nvme0n1p2 on a Linux laptop, /dev/disk3s1 on a Mac.) df -h ~ /tmp shows whether two folders sit on the same filesystem. For the second question, du adds up what is inside folders. Ask it about the project, including the hidden .pixi folder:


Terminal (laptop)

1du -sh ~/bioinf-computing/* ~/bioinf-computing/.pixi | sort -h


1

-s one total per name, -h human units. sort -h is like Chapter 6’s sort -n, but understands sizes such as 512K and 1.2G (with -n, 1.2G would sort before 512K).


4.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/NOTEBOOK.md
4.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/pixi.toml
4.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/README.md
8.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/logs
8.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/results
8.0K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/src
160K    /home/you/bioinf-computing/pixi.lock
4.3M    /home/you/bioinf-computing/data
1.3G    /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi
The book’s software is three hundred times bigger than its data. Real projects reverse that, but environments are never small, which is why they belong on storage with room for them (1).
Now name it. df answers “how full is this disk?”; du answers “how much is in these folders?”. Three details make du less obvious than it looks:

ls -l on a folder shows the size of its list of names (4096), not of its contents (Chapter 5); du measures the contents.
du reports space used on disk, rounded up to whole blocks, so a folder of small files uses more than the file sizes add up to: du -sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/run1 says 12K for files totalling 86 bytes (du -sh --apparent-size gives the sum of sizes).
Files can share space. pixi keeps downloaded packages in a cache (~/.cache/rattler on Linux) and links the environment’s files to it, so the same 1.3 GB shows up once: du -sh ~/.cache/rattler ~/bioinf-computing/.pixi counts it under whichever comes first (here 1.3G for the cache, then 97M for .pixi). PIXI_CACHE_DIR

moves the cache; it does not move an environment that already exists.


Table 7.10 gathers the questions.



Table 7.10: Disk questions and the commands that answer them.











Question
Command
Read
On a cluster




How full is the disk this folder is on?
df -h folder
Avail, Use%
often the whole shared system, not your share


What is big in here?
du -sh * .[!.]* \| sort -h
the last lines
run it on the folder you suspect, not on /


How big is one folder?
du -sh folder
the one total
slow on huge trees


What is my limit?
the site’s quota command or usage file
used vs limit
Chapter 10, Appendix A






(In the second row, .[!.]* matches hidden names such as .pixi without matching .., Chapter 5.)
On a cluster df on shared storage often shows the whole system, many terabytes or petabytes, not your share. On Nova, df -h ~ gives 172.16.7.238:/stor014/home  14T  7.5T  5.9T  56% /home: the home folders of everyone, on another machine (the address:/path form means network storage). Your real limit is a quota for your user or project, which each site reports its own way (Chapter 10, Appendix A). Table 7.11 compares two clusters.



Table 7.11: Checking storage limits on two clusters (captured November 2026).











Nova (ISU)
Ceres (SCINet; Atlas the same)




Quota command
none (quota -s prints nothing)
my_quotas: home and every project you belong to, usage vs quota in GB


Home limit
10 GB; check with du -sh ~
about 30 GB; my_quotas or quota -s


Group storage
/work/<group>; usage and quota in the file /work/<group>/group_storage_usage, updated hourly
/project/<name>; in my_quotas


df -h on group storage
shows the group’s share
shows the project’s quota as the size






So df can mislead in both directions: on one folder it shows the disk everyone shares, on another just your group’s allowance. Trust the site’s own command or file (ISU file storage, SCINet project management).
Quotas can also count files, not just bytes; df -i shows a whole filesystem’s file slots (inodes), which is likewise not your file-count quota. And du on a huge tree is slow and loads storage that everyone shares, so point it at the folder you suspect. ncdu, where installed, lets you browse sizes interactively.






TipFind what fills a folder



du -sh * .[!.]* | sort -h | tail -n 5 lists the five largest items in the current folder, hidden ones included. (If there are no hidden names, du says it cannot access .[!.]*: the pattern matched nothing and was passed on as it is, Chapter 5.)



Check yourself. df -h on a shared folder says 2.1P available, but your job fails with Disk quota exceeded. Why?






TipAnswer





There df describes the whole shared filesystem. Your group’s quota is a separate, much smaller limit; check it the way your site says, with a quota command or a usage file (Appendix A). It may also be a limit on the number of files.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.9 GNU (Linux) and BSD (macOS) tools
Chapter 1 promised this section. Each command below works on Linux and on a Mac after Chapter 1’s setup, but fails with a Mac’s own tools. Read each message and guess why before opening the answer:
$ ls --version
ls: unrecognized option `--version'
usage: ls [-@ABCFGHILOPRSTUWXabcdefghiklmnopqrstuvwxy1%,] [--color=when] [-D format] [file ...]
$ cat -A samples.csv
cat: illegal option -- A
usage: cat [-belnstuv] [file ...]
$ stat -c '%a' samples.csv
stat: illegal option -- c
usage: stat [-FLnq] [-f format | -l | -r | -s | -x] [-t timefmt] [file ...]
$ sed -i 's/x/y/' samples.csv
sed: 1: "samples.csv": unterminated substitute pattern






TipAnswer





These are the BSD versions of ls, cat, stat, and sed that come with macOS (captured on macOS 15 with /bin/bash 3.2 and the system’s own tools). They do not know --version, -A, or -c. BSD sed -i expects a suffix for a backup copy right after -i, so it took s/x/y/ as that suffix and the file name as the script: a confusing message about something you did not mean. With GNU tools first on PATH, the same commands work (ls --version prints ls (GNU coreutils) 9.11).



Now name it. The Linux systems you will use come with the GNU versions of the core tools this book uses: ls, cp, stat, sed, grep, find, awk, sort. (Not every Linux tool is GNU: ps and top usually come from a package called procps.) macOS comes with BSD versions: same names, mostly the same basic use, different options and messages. Chapter 1’s gnubin lines put GNU first on your Mac’s PATH, so the book’s commands work as written. To see which you have, use type -a (Section 7.4) or --version: GNU tools print a version, BSD tools usually reject the option.
A third family on new Ubuntu. From Ubuntu 25.10, and in 26.04 LTS (what WSL installs in late 2026), ls --version prints ls (uutils coreutils) 0.8.0. uutils is a rewrite of GNU’s core tools in the Rust language that aims to accept the same options; Ubuntu keeps GNU’s cp, mv, rm, and df, and grep and sed are still GNU (release notes). The book’s commands work there; a few messages read differently, as noted where they appear. Clusters still run GNU.
It still matters in three places:

Scripts from a colleague’s Mac, written for BSD tools (sed -i '', date -v), fail on Linux, and the book’s GNU commands fail on a Mac without the setup. The installed manual page (man sed) is the authority for what a Mac’s own tool does.
#!/bin/bash on a Mac means Apple’s bash 3.2, which lacks features from 2009 on that Chapter 8 may use. This book’s #!/usr/bin/env bash avoids it.
Minimal containers (Chapter 24) often have a third set, BusyBox, with fewer options still.




Table 7.12: Options you may meet that differ between GNU and BSD (overview).











Task
GNU (Linux)
BSD (macOS)
GNU form on a Mac’s own tools




Edit a file in place
sed -i 's/a/b/' f
sed -i '' 's/a/b/' f
a confusing sed: 1: … error


Show invisible characters
cat -A f
cat -et f
cat: illegal option -- A


Permissions as a number
stat -c '%a' f
stat -f '%Lp' f
stat: illegal option -- c


A date from text
date -d 2026-01-01
date -j -f %Y-%m-%d 2026-01-01
date: illegal option -- d


Perl-style regular expressions
grep -P
(none)
grep: invalid option -- P


Sizes as file lengths
du --apparent-size
du -A
du: unrecognized option






(Captured on macOS 15. Some older differences are gone: recent macOS has readlink -f, sort -h, and sort -V.)






Tip--version is a quick test



GNU tools answer --version; BSD tools usually refuse it. If a command’s options behave oddly on a Mac, check type -a first.



Check yourself. A colleague’s script runs sed -i 's/chr//' genes.bed and fails on a Mac without Chapter 1’s setup, with sed: 1: "genes.bed": …. Why?






TipAnswer





The Mac’s own sed is BSD sed, whose -i takes a backup suffix, so it read s/chr// as the suffix and the file name as the script. Use GNU sed (after the setup), or write sed -i '' 's/chr//' genes.bed for BSD only.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.10 Line endings: LF and CRLF
The practice folder from Chapter 5 has the same table twice: meta/samples.tsv (tab-separated) and meta/samples_from_excel.csv (comma-separated, as if saved from Excel). Ask both the same question: how many rows have 30 reads?


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share
1grep -c $'\t30$' meta/samples.tsv
grep -c ',30$' meta/samples_from_excel.csv


1

$'\t' is bash’s way to write a tab; $ in the pattern is the end of the line (Chapter 6).


2
0
No error, and the CSV gives the wrong answer. cat shows nothing odd:


Terminal (laptop)

cat meta/samples_from_excel.csv
cat -A meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 3
cat -A meta/samples.tsv | head -n 3

sample,run_folder,condition,reads
sample_C,Run 3 final,treated,12
sample_A,run1,control,9
sample_B,run2,control,30
sample_E,run5,treated,105
sample_B,run2,control,30
sample_D,run4,control,8
sample,run_folder,condition,reads^M$
sample_C,Run 3 final,treated,12^M$
sample_A,run1,control,9^M$
sample^Irun_folder^Icondition^Ireads$
sample_C^IRun 3 final^Itreated^I12$
sample_A^Irun1^Icontrol^I9$
cat -A (Chapter 6 used it to show tabs as ^I) marks each line end with $. In the CSV every line ends in ^M$: an invisible carriage return character (\r) before the newline. So the line ends in 30\r, not 30, and ,30$ does not match (Figure 7.7).




  Line endings, and why a Windows-saved CSV breaks a pattern match. Top, the same last line of a table, ending in the bytes 3 and 0: as TSV with Unix endings, sample_B, tab, run2, tab, control, tab, 30 ends in one byte, \n (line feed); as CSV saved on Windows, sample_B,run2,control,30 ends in two bytes, \r\n, where \r (carriage return) is the extra one. Middle, cat shows both lines clean, because \r is invisible; cat -A shows tabs as ^I, \r as ^M, and each line end as $, giving sample_B^Irun2^Icontrol^I30$ and sample_B,run2,control,30^M$. Bottom, how a command splits the CSV line into fields: field 2, run2, is clean, but the last field is 30\r, not 30, so grep ',30$' finds 0 lines.
  
  
  1 · The same last line, with the bytes at its end
  
  TSV
  Linux, macOS
  sample_B⇥run2⇥control⇥
  
    
    
  
  
  
    3
    0
    \n
  
  \n = LF, line feed:
  one byte ends the line
  
  CSV
  saved on Windows
  sample_B,run2,control,
  
    
    
  
  
  
  
    3
    0
    \r
    \n
  
  \r\n = CRLF: \r, carriage return,
  is an extra, invisible byte
  
  
  2 · What you see
  CAT FILE
  CAT -A FILE
  TSV
  sample_B        run2    control 30
  sample_B^Irun2^Icontrol^I30$
  CSV
  sample_B,run2,control,30
  sample_B,run2,control,30^M$
  both look clean: \r prints nothing
  ^I tab · ^M \r · $ end of line
  
  
  3 · What a command reads from the CSV line
  
    field 1
    field 2
    field 3
    field 4 (last)
  
  
  
  
  
  
    sample_B
    run2
    control
    30\r
  
  
    ,
    ,
    ,
  
  ✓ clean
  ✗ 30\r, not 30
  grep ',30$' finds 0 lines: $ wants the line to end right after 30, but \r comes first




Figure 7.7: The same row in the two files. cat shows them alike; cat -A shows the CSV’s extra carriage return (^M), which sticks to the last field, so a pattern anchored at the line end finds nothing.



The damage sticks to the last field. Fields in the middle are clean; the last one carries the \r:


Terminal (laptop)

cut -d, -f2 meta/samples_from_excel.csv | head -n 3 | cat -A
1f=$(sed -n 3p meta/samples_from_excel.csv | cut -d, -f4)
2printf '%q\n' "$f"
[ "$f" = 9 ] && echo same || echo different


1

Store the reads field of line 3 in f. $( ) and variables are Chapter 8; copy this as it is.

2

%q prints a value with invisible characters spelled out.


run_folder$
Run 3 final$
run1$
$'9\r'
different
The value is 9\r, so a comparison with 9 is silently false. When the last column holds file names, the result is a “missing” file that is plainly there. A two-line sheet in scratch shows it:


Terminal (laptop)

cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
printf 'sample,fastq_1\r\nWT_REP1,SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz\r\n' > sheet.csv
ls ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw/$(tail -n 1 sheet.csv | cut -d, -f2)

ls: cannot access '/home/you/bioinf-computing/data/raw/SRR6357070_1.fastq.gz'$'\r': No such file or directory
GNU ls spells out the $'\r'; many tools print a name that looks exactly right. And a script saved with CRLF fails on its first line, because the shebang now names a program called bash\r:


Terminal (laptop)

printf '%s\r\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'echo "hello"' > crlf.sh
chmod u+x crlf.sh
./crlf.sh

/usr/bin/env: ‘bash\r’: No such file or directory
/usr/bin/env: use -[v]S to pass options in shebang lines
(The second line is env guessing at a different problem; ignore it. Older env, such as Nova’s, prints only the first line. Ubuntu 26.04’s env writes it as env: $'bash\r': No such file or directory; on a Mac it is env: bash\r: No such file or directory. With #!/bin/bash instead, bash 5.1 (Nova) and 5.3 say /bin/bash^M: bad interpreter: No such file or directory, with status 126 instead of 127: the ^M is the carriage return. Bash 5.2 says only cannot execute: required file not found, which is even less helpful.)
How to detect it. Look with cat -A (for ^M), and count with grep -c $'\r' file, which prints how many lines contain a carriage return: 7 for the CSV, 0 for the TSV. Do not rely on file: it reports with CRLF line terminators for some text (file crlf.sh does), but once it recognises a CSV it says only CSV ASCII text, with or without carriage returns (Ubuntu’s file 5.45; macOS’s and Nova’s 5.39 say CSV text). On a two-line CSV saved by Excel, file did mention CRLF; on the seven-line sheet it did not, so its answer depends on the file.
Now name it. Linux and macOS end each line with one character, a line feed (LF, \n). Windows ends lines with two, carriage return + line feed (CRLF, \r\n). CRLF is normal in CSV files, and proper CSV readers in R and Python handle it (Chapter 14); what breaks is a shell tool or simple script that keeps the \r as part of the last field. Files get CRLF endings from Windows editors, Excel’s “Save as CSV”, and email attachments. In WSL, files under /mnt/c (Chapter 1’s pitfall) are often edited with Windows programs, which is where the CRLF comes from; the folder itself does not change the bytes. Excel’s CSV UTF-8 format also puts three invisible bytes, a byte order mark, before the first column name: cat -A shows M-oM-;M-?sample,reads^M$, and a shell tool then sees a first column called something other than sample. sed '1s/^\xEF\xBB\xBF//' removes it; R’s and Python’s CSV readers handle it.
Fix it by deleting the \r at each line end. Write a fixed copy first and check it:


Terminal (laptop)

sed 's/\r$//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv > samples_lf.csv
grep -c $'\r' samples_lf.csv
echo $?
grep -c ',30$' samples_lf.csv

0
1
2
No carriage returns left, and the count is right. The 1 from echo $? is not a failure: grep exits with 1 when it finds no matching lines, which is what you wanted here (Chapter 8 returns to this). Once you trust the command, GNU sed -i 's/\r$//' file fixes a file in place: on your own copy, never on data/raw/ (Chapter 6). Two other tools you will see: tr -d '\r' < in > out deletes every carriage return, not only those at line ends (fine for a sample sheet), and dos2unix file, where installed, does the same job as sed. Line-ending fixes are for text files only, never for compressed or binary data.



Table 7.13: Line endings by system.












System
Line ending
Bytes
cat -A shows
Convert with




Linux, macOS
LF
\n
$
(already right)


Windows
CRLF
\r\n
^M$
sed 's/\r$//' in > out


Classic Mac OS (before 2001)
CR
\r
one long line with ^M
tr '\r' '\n' < in > out






Prevent it where you can. VS Code shows LF or CRLF in the status bar at the bottom of the window; click it to change a file, and set "files.eol": "\n" in your settings to make LF the default (VS Code docs). Git can convert line endings for you (Chapter 21). Before a pipeline run, check sample sheets with grep -c $'\r' (Chapter 26). One more invisible character from Excel, the byte-order mark at the start of a file, is Chapter 36.






WarningPitfall: CRLF from Windows or Excel



Files from Windows or Excel can end lines in CRLF. Shell tools then see a \r stuck to the last field, and matches and comparisons fail silently. Check with cat -A (look for ^M) or grep -c $'\r' before a script reads them.








CautionMisconception: “A CSV file is a CSV file; where it was saved doesn’t matter”



Reality. The program and system that saved it decide its line endings (and whether it starts with an invisible byte-order mark). A \r at each line end sticks to the last field, so matches and comparisons on it fail without an error.



Check yourself. cat -A samples.csv shows ^M$ at every line end. Name one way it got that way and one fix.






TipAnswer





It was saved by Excel or a Windows editor. Fix: sed 's/\r$//' samples.csv > samples_lf.csv, check with grep -c $'\r' samples_lf.csv (prints 0), then use the new file.

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.11 Summary

A permission string is a type letter and three triplets (user, group, other) of r, w, x; each triplet is also one octal digit (4 + 2 + 1). On a folder, r lists names, x reaches the entries, and w with x adds or removes them, so deleting a file depends on its folder. chmod changes permissions; read the string and change one letter, never 777.
A script runs as a command with a shebang line (#!/usr/bin/env bash) and the x bit. Permission denied (126) means found but not runnable; command not found (127) means not on PATH.
Bash checks aliases, functions, and builtins, then searches the PATH folders in order and runs the first match; type -a shows them all. pixi run and module load work by putting a folder first on PATH.
export passes a variable to the programs a shell starts; a line in ~/.bashrc sets it for every new terminal. Login shells read the first of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile; in the book’s setup that file reads ~/.bashrc. Back up before editing, and keep it silent.
A process has a PID and a parent. Ctrl-CCtrl-C and kill ask it to end, kill -9 forces it, Ctrl-ZCtrl-Z only pauses it. df shows how full a disk is, du what is in folders; on a cluster your limit is a quota. GNU and BSD tools share names but not options. Windows line endings leave a \r on the last field: find it with cat -A or grep -c $'\r', remove it with sed 's/\r$//'.




Table 7.14: The chapter’s commands on one page.









Task
Command




Who am I, which groups
whoami, id


Read permissions
ls -l, ls -ld folder, stat -c '%A %a %n' f


Change permissions
chmod u+x f, chmod a-w f, chmod 644 f, chmod 700 d, chmod -R g+rX d


Make a script run
#!/usr/bin/env bash on line 1, chmod u+x script.sh, ./script.sh


What runs, from where
type -a name, echo "$PATH" \| tr ':' '\n', hash -r


Add a folder to PATH
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"


Variables
NAME=value cmd, export NAME=value, env, locale


Startup files
~/.bashrc; cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07; source ~/.bashrc


Processes
cmd &, jobs, fg, bg, ps, ps -u "$USER", top, kill %1, kill PID, kill -9 PID


Disk
df -h folder, du -sh * .[!.]* \| sort -h


Which tools
type -a ls, ls --version


Line endings
cat -A f, grep -c $'\r' f, sed 's/\r$//' in > out

title: 7  The Linux system
text:
7.12 Exercises
Do these in ~/bioinf-computing-ch07. Exercise 4 is the only one that changes a file outside it (your ~/.bashrc, after a backup).

Exercise 1. Make a broken tool run. A labmate’s script, count_lines.sh, prints a file’s name and its number of lines. It arrived from a Windows laptop with a sample sheet. Set up the copy (the printf writes the script with Windows line endings, and chmod 644 makes sure it starts out not executable):


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07
printf '%s\r\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' \
  '# count_lines.sh: print a file name and its number of lines' \
  'printf "%s: %s lines\n" "$(basename "$1")" "$(wc -l < "$1")"' \
  > bin/count_lines.sh
chmod 644 bin/count_lines.sh
cp ~/bioinf-computing-ch05/share/meta/samples_from_excel.csv samples.csv

The goal: from any folder, count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv prints samples.csv: 7 lines. Fix one fault at a time, using only the message, and run the script by its path until the last step:

Run ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv. Fix what the message says.
Run the same command again. Fix what the new message says.
Run it once more: it should work.
cd ~ and run it by name: count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv. Make that work for this terminal.

Then the sample sheet: count its rows with 30 reads (grep -c ',30$') and its carriage returns (grep -c $'\r'), fix it in place with GNU sed -i, and count again. Record each message and fix in NOTEBOOK.md. (The script’s $1, $( ), and basename are Chapter 8; you only need to make it run.)






TipAnswer





$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
bash: ./bin/count_lines.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod u+x bin/count_lines.sh
$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
/usr/bin/env: ‘bash\r’: No such file or directory
/usr/bin/env: use -[v]S to pass options in shebang lines
$ sed -i 's/\r$//' bin/count_lines.sh
$ ./bin/count_lines.sh samples.csv
samples.csv: 7 lines
$ cd ~
$ count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
bash: count_lines.sh: command not found
$ export PATH="$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch07/bin:$PATH"
$ count_lines.sh ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
samples.csv: 7 lines

No x bit (126): chmod u+x. 2. Windows line endings in the shebang, so env looked for bash\r (127): remove the \r. 4. The folder is not on PATH (127): add it, for this terminal only.

The sheet:
$ grep -c ',30$' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
0
$ grep -c $'\r' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
7
$ sed -i 's/\r$//' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
$ grep -c ',30$' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
2
$ grep -c $'\r' ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/samples.csv
0
The line count was 7 before and after: wc -l counts line ends, and a carriage return does not change how many there are. Only the \r count shows that the fix worked. (echo $? after the last grep gives 1, “no lines matched”, which is the result you wanted.)





Exercise 2. Read and set permissions. In ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2/, make notes.txt, run.sh, and a folder private/. Set them to -rw-r--r--, -rwxr-xr-x, and drwx------: once with symbolic chmod, then again from the start with octal. Check with ls -l and stat -c '%A %a %n'. Then explain, from ls -ld ~/bioinf-computing/data/raw, why rm on a raw file fails.






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2 && cd ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/perm2
touch notes.txt run.sh && mkdir private
chmod u+x,go+rx run.sh              # from -rw-r--r--: add x for all, r for group and other
chmod go-rx private                 # from drwxr-xr-x
stat -c '%A %a %n' notes.txt run.sh private
chmod 644 notes.txt && chmod 755 run.sh && chmod 700 private

-rw-r--r-- 644 notes.txt
-rwxr-xr-x 755 run.sh
drwx------ 700 private
notes.txt already had 644 from the umask. data/raw is dr-xr-xr-x: nobody has w on the folder, and removing a file changes the folder, so rm is refused even with -f.





Exercise 3. Which copy runs? Make a fake seqkit that only prints a version, put its folder first on PATH in this terminal, and see which copy each command finds:


Terminal (laptop)

mkdir -p ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin
printf '%s\n' '#!/usr/bin/env bash' 'echo "seqkit v0.0.1 (fake)"' > ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
chmod u+x ~/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
export PATH="$HOME/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin:$PATH"
type -a seqkit
seqkit version
cd ~/bioinf-computing
pixi run bash -c 'type -a seqkit; seqkit version'

Which copy runs in each case, and why? Close the terminal afterwards to undo the PATH change. (Do not put this in ~/.bashrc.)






TipAnswer





seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
seqkit v0.0.1 (fake)
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing/.pixi/envs/default/bin/seqkit
seqkit is /home/you/bioinf-computing-ch07/fakebin/seqkit
seqkit v2.14.0
In the plain terminal, fakebin is first on PATH, so bare seqkit is the fake. (If another seqkit is installed on your machine, type -a lists it below.) Under pixi run, the environment’s folder goes in front of everything, so the real seqkit wins, and type -a shows the fake one second. This is why the book always writes pixi run seqkit.





Exercise 4. Make a setting permanent. Back up ~/.bashrc with cp -n, then add export EDITOR=nano (and, on a cluster where 1 told you to, the PIXI_CACHE_DIR line) if it is not there yet. Prove it works in a new terminal and, if you have a cluster account, in a new SSH login. Record in NOTEBOOK.md which of ~/.bash_profile, ~/.bash_login, ~/.profile, and ~/.bashrc exist on each machine, and which one reads ~/.bashrc.






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

cp -n ~/.bashrc ~/.bashrc.bak-ch07
1grep -n 'EDITOR=' ~/.bashrc
grep -qxF 'export EDITOR=nano' ~/.bashrc ||
2  echo 'export EDITOR=nano' >> ~/.bashrc
ls -a ~ | grep -E '^\.(bash|profile)'
grep -n bashrc ~/.bash_profile ~/.bash_login ~/.profile 2>/dev/null


1

Look first. If an active line (not starting with #) already sets EDITOR to something else, change that line in nano rather than adding a second one.

2

-x matches whole lines only, -F treats the text as plain text, not a pattern, and -q prints nothing. The || adds the line only if that exact line is missing, so running it twice does not add it twice. A commented-out # export EDITOR=vim does not count.


A later line wins over an earlier one, so the real check is a new terminal, where echo "$EDITOR" prints nano. On Ubuntu and WSL you will usually find ~/.profile reading ~/.bashrc; on a Mac, ~/.bash_profile from Chapter 1. If the SSH login does not see the setting, the cluster’s login file does not read ~/.bashrc (see the check in Section 7.6).





Exercise 5. Find and end a process; find the space. Start sleep 600 &, find its PID with ps and in top, end it with kill, and confirm with jobs. Then list the five largest items in ~/bioinf-computing, hidden ones included. Which is the environment, and why is it so large compared with the data?






TipAnswer







Terminal (laptop)

sleep 600 &
ps
kill %1          # or: kill <the PID from ps>
jobs
cd ~/bioinf-computing
du -sh * .[!.]* | sort -h | tail -n 5

In top, look for sleep in the COMMAND column (press q to quit). The largest item is .pixi (about 1.3 GB on Linux): Python, R, and seqkit with every library they need, for one operating system. The data are a few megabytes. Real projects have far more data, but environments are always this kind of size, which is why pixi’s cache and environments go on project storage on a cluster (1).

title: Report an Issue
text:
Which route for what
Quick links: report an error · something doesn’t run · ask a question · suggest an idea · open issues
A computing book goes wrong in more ways than most: a command that worked last year fails with a new tool version, a cluster behaves differently from the one the book was tested on, a download link moves, an install breaks on one operating system. The fastest way to find these is readers. Every report is read, and the fix goes onto the website as soon as it is made.
There is no errata list. When something is wrong it is corrected in the book itself.
Issues and Discussions are kept separate on purpose. The issue tracker holds only things with a fix, so it reads as a to-do list and you can search it to see whether your problem is already reported. Questions go to Discussions because a question is not a defect, but a run of questions on the same section is a sign the explanation failed, and that does become an issue.

title: Report an Issue
text:
You have found
Use




A wrong command, output, or claim
An issue, using the Error in the book form


A command or install that fails for you (pixi, VS Code, a tool, a cluster step)
An issue, using the Something doesn’t run form


A broken link, moved download, or outdated tool version
An issue, using the Error in the book form


A typo or awkward sentence you are willing to fix
A pull request (see below)


A typo you would rather just report
The Error in the book form


A section you did not follow, or are not sure is right
A question in Discussions › Q&A


A suggestion: a better example, a missing topic or tool
An idea in Discussions › Ideas


Something that should not be public
Email the author (the address on the GitHub profile)

title: Report an Issue
text:
Before you report
Note the page. Copy the URL of the page and the section heading. The book changes often while it is being written, so say roughly when you read it.
Search the open issues. If someone has already reported it, add a comment there rather than opening a second one. A second report on the same problem is still useful: it says how many readers it affects.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Reporting an error
You need a free GitHub account. The Error in the book form asks for:

Chapter and section, with the command, code chunk, table, or figure if there is one.
What is wrong (quote it as it appears) and what it should be.
How you know. Optional, and the most useful field: the command you ran and its output, or a link to the tool’s documentation.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Reporting something that doesn’t run
Problems with installs and commands are the most common reports, and the hardest to fix without details. The Something doesn’t run form asks for:

Where you ran it: laptop, cluster login node, or compute node; the operating system (macOS, Windows with WSL2, or Linux); the cluster name if there is one (e.g., SCINet Ceres, ISU Nova).
The exact command, copied, not retyped.
The complete error message, copied as text, not a screenshot, and not shortened. The useful line is often the first error, not the last.
Your environment: the output of pixi info run in the book’s folder. On a cluster, also any module load lines you ran first.

Three more fields are optional but often save a round of questions:

What you expected, for example the output the book shows.
What you have tried: anything you checked or changed, and what happened.
The version of the failing tool, for example the output of pixi run seqkit version. pixi info describes the environment but does not list the versions of the tools in it.







WarningPitfall



Never paste passwords, SSH private keys, access tokens, or private data into an issue. Issues are public and stay public. Replace usernames, paths, and hostnames you would rather not share with placeholders such as <user>.

title: Report an Issue
text:
Fixing it yourself
For a typo or a wording fix, the fastest route is to make the change and propose it on GitHub:

Open the page’s source file in the repository. Chapters live in chapters/, one .qmd file each (Markdown with code), named by number: chapter 5 is chapters/05-shell-basics.qmd.
Click the pencil icon. GitHub offers to fork the repository into your own account; accept.
Make the change, write one line saying what it is, and choose Propose changes, then Create pull request.

The author reviews it, and merges it or asks for a change. Some things to know before you edit:

Edit the .qmd only. _book/ is generated output.
One fix per pull request. A three-line change is reviewed in a minute; a change that touches four chapters waits.
Do not add to references.bib unless you have checked the DOI. Every entry in it has been verified.
Your contribution is offered under the book’s licenses: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for text and figures, MIT for code.
Larger changes (a rewritten section, a new example) should start as a discussion in Ideas, so the shape is agreed before the work is done.

title: Report an Issue
section: Asking a question or suggesting something
text:
Asking a question or suggesting something
Discussions › Q&A is for “I did not follow this step” or “is this right?”. Other readers can answer as well as the author, and an answered question stays there for the next person.
Discussions › Ideas is for a different example, a tool the book should cover, or a better way to explain something. Scope is the author’s call: this book aims for awareness, not depth, and full algorithms belong to the other books in the series. The discussion is where the case is made.

title: Report an Issue
text:
What happens next
A report is labelled with its chapter and its type (error, typo, doesnt-run, link). The fix is made on the main branch and the website updates from it. If a problem only affects one operating system or cluster, the fix may be a note in the chapter rather than a change to the command.

title: Appendix A — Cluster sites: SCINet and Nova
text:
Who can get an account, and how to apply (SCINet for USDA-affiliated users; ISU Nova for Iowa State users); how long approval takes
Logging in: host names, multi-factor authentication, first login, published host-key fingerprints
Data transfer nodes: Nova novadtn.its.iastate.edu; SCINet ceres-dtn.scinet.usda.gov, atlas-dtn.hpc.msstate.edu; Globus
Storage areas, quotas, and what is backed up (home, project, scratch)
Nova quotas (checked 2026-11-20): no quota command (quota -s prints nothing; the documented cdw is missing; my_workdir lower-cases the group and fails for /work/ABG). Home 10 GB, check with du -sh ~. Group: cat /work/<group>/group_storage_usage (group NAME AVAIL USED, fraction used, then per user TYPE NAME USED QUOTA OBJUSED OBJQUOTA, where OBJ counts files); df -h /work/<group> shows the same group share
Ceres quotas (checked 2026-11-20): my_quotas (/usr/local/bin) lists home, each /project/<name>, and Juno /LTS/project/<name>, with columns Path, Usage (GB), Quota (GB), Availible (GB) (sic), Consumed (%), Status; home about 30 GB (quota -s also works for home: 30518M quota, 50545M limit, no file limit); /90daydata has no quota but deletes data 90 days after last access; df -h /project/<name> shows the project’s quota as the size
Atlas (checked 2026-11-21): Rocky Linux 9.6, bash 5.1.8, umask 0027, Ctrl-Z on. my_quotas is /apps/bin/my_quotas (same columns, spelled Available; sections Atlas home directory, Atlas working project space; no Juno), home 30 GB; projects have separate, smaller allocations from Ceres. df -h ~ shows the whole /atlas/home (6.8P), not your share; quota -s fails with Operation not permitted on /atlas/90daydata. Atlas /project/<name> is drwxrws--- (root, proj-<name>; setgid, no sticky, no SELinux label); new files -rw-r----- with the project group; df -h /project/<name> shows the project quota (1.1T for a 1,000 GB allocation)
Shared group folders: Nova /work/<group> is drwxrws--T, owned by root and the lab’s group (setgid on, sticky, closed to others); new files take the lab’s group and, with Nova’s umask 0002, are group-writable (captured 2026-11-20). Ceres /project/<name> is also drwxrws--T (root, group proj-<name>); new files take proj-<name> but, with SCINet’s umask 0027, are -rw-r----- (group reads, cannot edit); your primary group is a personal one (captured 2026-11-20)
Ceres vs Atlas: one comparison table (login, DTN, and OnDemand hosts; separate storage and quotas for the same projects; OnDemand apps; hardware and partitions; location), checked against SCINet’s pages
Software on the site: modules, containers, and where pixi fits
VS Code on each site: the supported route (Nova: VS Code Tunnel app or VS Code Server in Open OnDemand, Remote-SSH only to compute nodes; SCINet: VS Code Server in Open OnDemand or a registered tunnel to Ceres compute nodes), what each needs (VPN; Microsoft or GitHub account), ending a session to release its resources, and moving the code-server folder from $HOME to project storage
Sources: ISU: Using VS Code on the cluster, SCINet: VS Code guide
Where to get help: each site’s own documentation and support contacts
